guideCitation.keyPoint: Multiple painless submandibular/cervical nodes with B-symptom weight loss require urgent biopsy and TB evaluation to distinguish lymphoma from tuberculous lymphadenitis.

sourceStation.title: Submental & Submandibular Lymphadenopathy
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2. A boy presented with loss of weight of 10 kg over 3 months. On examination he had multiple lumps in the submental and submandibular area.
2.1 Give 2 disorders which can give rise to this condition.  [Photo omitted on slide in original Drive PPTX]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Lymphoma (Hodgkin or Non-Hodgkin lymphoma — 'B symptoms' of weight loss); (2) Tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula); (3) Metastatic malignancy or Infectious mononucleosis / HIV.

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, mild abdominal distension, and the symmetrical non-blanching palpable rash over his lower limbs shown in the photograph. Which pathophysiological mechanism best accounts for his abdominal pain?
options: Small-vessel IgA vasculitis causing bowel wall oedema or intussusception
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura causing spontaneous retroperitoneal haematoma
Meningococcal septicaemia producing bilateral adrenal haemorrhage
Acute appendicitis complicated by generalised faecal peritonitis
Gallstone impaction at the ampulla of Vater causing acute pancreatitis
optionRationales: Correct: Symmetrical palpable purpura over the legs and buttocks with colicky abdominal pain defines Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), where mesenteric leukocytoclastic vasculitis causes submucosal oedema/haemorrhage and may act as a lead point for intussusception.
Incorrect: ITP causes flat, non-palpable petechiae and ecchymoses with severe thrombocytopenia, whereas platelet counts are normal or elevated in palpable purpuric vasculitis.
Incorrect: Meningococcaemia causes toxic shock, meningism, and rapidly coalescing retiform purpura rather than symmetrical dependent palpable purpura in a stable patient.
Incorrect: Acute appendicitis presents with migratory right iliac fossa tenderness and fever without a symmetrical lower-limb palpable purpuric eruption.
Incorrect: Biliary pancreatitis produces severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with jaundice rather than dependent palpable lower-limb purpura.
clinicalPearl: In Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), always monitor urine microscopy/proteinuria for IgA nephritis and obtain an abdominal ultrasound if vomiting or distension persists to exclude ileo-ileal intussusception.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Dependent palpable purpura with abdominal pain signifies IgA vasculitis (HSP), driven by mesenteric small-vessel vasculitis with risk of submucosal bleeding and intussusception.

sourceStation.title: Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (IgA Vasculitis)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. A 17-year-old boy presented with abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination he had abdominal distension and his legs were as shown in the given picture.
3.1 What is the most likely diagnosis?
3.2 What is the reason for abdominal pain?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (3.1) Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis). (3.2) Cause of abdominal pain: Mesenteric / bowel wall small-vessel IgA vasculitis causing submucosal oedema/haemorrhage (and risk of intussusception or bowel ischaemia).

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: Twenty minutes after an intravenous antibiotic dose, a 28-year-old woman develops the pruritic raised erythematous plaques shown in the photograph, followed by hoarseness, stridor, and a blood pressure of 75/45 mmHg. Which immediate medication is the first-line life-saving treatment?
options: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg slow bolus
Intravenous chlorpheniramine 10 mg over 1 minute
Subcutaneous adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:10,000) in forearm
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000)
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg via face mask
optionRationales: Incorrect: Intravenous hydrocortisone has a delayed onset of hours and serves only as a second-line adjunct to reduce biphasic reactions after IM adrenaline.
Incorrect: Antihistamines relieve cutaneous pruritus and urticaria but cannot reverse life-threatening airway oedema or distributive shock.
Incorrect: Subcutaneous absorption is erratic and slow during shock, and 1:10,000 is the dilute formulation reserved for monitored IV use in peri-arrest settings.

Correct: Acute urticaria progressing to laryngeal stridor and hypotension defines anaphylaxis; immediate IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh reverses bronchospasm, mucosal oedema, and vasodilatory shock.
Incorrect: Nebulised beta-agonists may supplement bronchodilation once adrenaline is given, but alone they fail to treat hypotension or upper airway oedema.
clinicalPearl: For anaphylaxis in Kelaniya Emergency OSCEs, state the exact dose, concentration, and site: 0.5 mL of 1:1000 (500 micrograms) adrenaline IM into the anterolateral mid-thigh immediately, repeated every 5 minutes if needed, alongside IV fluids, hydrocortisone, and chlorpheniramine.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Anaphylaxis accompanying acute urticaria requires immediate 0.5 mg IM adrenaline (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh before IV hydrocortisone and antihistamines.

sourceStation.title: Urticaria & Anaphylaxis Emergency
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4.
4.1 What is the emergency that is associated with the above skin lesion?
4.2 Name 3 medications that can be given to manage this.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Anaphylaxis (acute life-threatening airway/laryngeal oedema, bronchospasm, distributive shock). (4.2) Medications: (1) IM Adrenaline (Epinephrine) 1:1000 (0.5 mg = 0.5 mL IM anterolateral thigh — first-line!); (2) IV Hydrocortisone (200 mg); (3) IV/Oral Antihistamine (e.g., Chlorpheniramine 10 mg IV) ± nebulised salbutamol if bronchospasm.

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 42-year-old woman complains of burning mouth soreness when eating spicy food and increasing exertional fatigue. Examination of her tongue reveals the appearance shown in the photograph. Which finding and primary underlying pathology best match this picture?
options: Oral hairy leukoplakia; Epstein-Barr virus reactivation
Geographic tongue; benign migratory oral mucositis
Black hairy tongue; prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics
Pseudomembranous candidiasis; inhaled corticosteroid therapy
Atrophic glossitis; iron, folate, or B12 deficiency
optionRationales: Incorrect: Oral hairy leukoplakia produces adherent, corrugated white plaques along the lateral tongue borders in immunocompromised patients rather than diffuse papillary atrophy.
Incorrect: Geographic tongue exhibits irregular map-like erythematous patches surrounded by raised serpiginous white borders rather than uniform smooth depapillation.
Incorrect: Black hairy tongue involves hypertrophy and dark keratin staining of elongated filiform papillae rather than loss of papillae.
Incorrect: Oral thrush presents as curdy white plaques that scrape off leaving a raw erythematous base rather than a uniformly smooth, bald tongue.
Correct: A smooth, shiny, beefy-red depapillated tongue resulting from loss of filiform papillae is atrophic glossitis, classically caused by iron deficiency (or vitamin B12/folate deficiency).
clinicalPearl: When examining a patient with a smooth depapillated tongue (atrophic glossitis), also inspect the mouth corners for angular cheilitis, conjunctivae for pallor, and fingernails for koilonychia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Smooth, erythematous, depapillated tongue (atrophic glossitis) points to iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiency anaemia.

sourceStation.title: Atrophic Glossitis (Nutritional Anaemia)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5.
5.1 Name 2 abnormalities that can be seen in this picture.
5.2 What is the most likely underlying pathology?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Abnormalities: Smooth, bald, erythematous tongue (atrophic glossitis / loss of filiform papillae) and pallor / angular cheilitis. (5.2) Underlying pathology: Iron deficiency anaemia (also Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency).

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive painless loss of sensation in both hands over several years, leading to recurrent unnoticed thermal burns and the bilateral digital shortening and facial changes shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis mutilans
Multibacillary lepromatous leprosy
Sclerodactyly with acro-osteolysis
Psoriatic arthritis mutilans
Diabetic distal polyneuropathy
optionRationales: Incorrect: Arthritis mutilans produces telescoping 'opera-glass' joints from severe osteolysis with painful inflammatory synovitis rather than painless sensory loss and lagophthalmos.

Correct: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss from peripheral nerve trunk damage, trophic ulcers causing auto-amputation/resorption of digits, facial infiltration, and ocular lagophthalmos are classic for advanced multibacillary lepromatous leprosy.
Incorrect: Systemic sclerosis produces sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon, and microstomia with preserved distal pain and temperature sensation.
Incorrect: Psoriatic arthritis mutilans causes severe joint destruction accompanied by cutaneous plaques and nail dystrophy rather than neuropathic anaesthetic digits.
Incorrect: Diabetic neuropathy rarely causes bilateral upper-limb digital auto-amputation together with facial skin infiltration and ocular ectropion.
clinicalPearl: Always palpate superficial peripheral nerves (ulnar at the medial epicondyle, common peroneal at the fibular neck, and great auricular nerve) for thickening and tenderness whenever sensory neuropathy and trophic digital loss are present.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Leprosy causes thickened peripheral nerves (notably ulnar and facial/ophthalmic branches) leading to glove-and-stocking anaesthesia, trophic ulceration, and clawing.

sourceStation.title: Lepromatous Leprosy
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 01
This 40-year-old woman presented with loss of sensations of both hands.
What is the likely diagnosis? (10 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Lepromatous leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae multibacillary disease).

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive cosmetic and structural nail changes across multiple fingers as shown in the photograph, including pinpoint nail plate depressions, distal nail-bed separation, and thickened subungual debris. Which underlying disorder is most strongly associated with these findings?
options: Iron deficiency anaemia
Chronic plaque psoriasis
Chronic liver cirrhosis
Subacute infective endocarditis
Chronic kidney disease
optionRationales: Incorrect: Severe chronic iron deficiency causes flat nails (platynychia) and spoon-shaped koilonychia rather than coarse pitting and subungual hyperkeratosis.

Correct: The triad of nail pitting (thimble pitting), distal onycholysis with 'oil-drop' salmon patches, and subungual hyperkeratosis is characteristic of psoriatic nail dystrophy and predicts psoriatic arthritis.
Incorrect: Cirrhosis is associated with white nail beds with narrow distal pink bands (Terry nails) and leukonychia.
Incorrect: Infective endocarditis causes finger clubbing and linear longitudinal splinter haemorrhages beneath the nail plate rather than pitting and subungual hyperkeratosis.
Incorrect: Chronic uraemia classically produces 'half-and-half' (Lindsay) nails with a white proximal half and reddish-brown distal band.
clinicalPearl: In a Rheumatology/Dermatology CSS station, psoriatic nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis) is strongly linked with DIP-predominant psoriatic arthritis—always inspect hidden extensor elbows, scalp, and natal cleft.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Nail pitting, distal onycholysis, and subungual hyperkeratosis constitute classic psoriatic nail disease.

sourceStation.title: Psoriatic Nail Changes
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Question 04
A woman presented to you and she is worried about the condition of her nails.
4.1 Write 3 features you observe in these nails. (6 marks)
4.2 State the condition where you see these features in nails. (4 marks)
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Nail pitting, Subungual hyperkeratosis, and Onycholysis. (4.2) Condition: Psoriasis (psoriatic nail dystrophy).

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 52-year-old man from a coastal district in Sri Lanka presents with chronic, progressive, non-pitting swelling and thickened verrucous skin folds of his right lower limb as shown in the photograph. Which complication is he at greatest ongoing risk of developing?
options: Iliofemoral deep venous thrombosis with saddle embolism
Necrotising fasciitis due to Clostridium perfringens
Acute osteofascial compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy
Recurrent bacterial cellulitis and acute dermatolymphangioadenitis
Spontaneous popliteal arterial aneurysm rupture
optionRationales: Incorrect: Elephantiasis represents chronic lymphatic obstruction rather than acute deep venous thrombosis, so recurrent skin sepsis—not saddle PE—is the hallmark recurring complication.
Incorrect: Gas gangrene is an acute traumatic/surgical anaerobic emergency rather than the typical chronic recurrent infective complication of filarial lymphoedema.
Incorrect: Chronic interstitial fibrotic lymphoedema develops gradually over years without acute raised intracompartmental muscle pressure.

Correct: Chronic filarial lymphoedema (elephantiasis, classically caused by Wuchereria bancrofti in Sri Lanka) impairs local lymphatic drainage and skin barrier integrity, predisposing to recurrent episodes of acute dermatolymphangioadenitis/bacterial cellulitis and fungal intertrigo.
Incorrect: Arterial aneurysms are unrelated to chronic lymphatic obstruction caused by filarial nematodes.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis), meticulous daily limb washing, skin-fold drying, antifungal treatment of toe-web maceration, limb elevation, and prompt antibiotics for acute dermatolymphangioadenitis prevent progression.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Chronic lower-limb lymphoedema (elephantiasis) predisposes to recurrent secondary bacterial cellulitis and fungal skin-fold infections requiring strict limb hygiene.

sourceStation.title: Right Lower Limb Elephantiasis (Lymphatic Filariasis)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05.
5.1 State the diagnosis.
5.2 State a complication of this condition.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (5.1) Right lower limb elephantiasis (chronic lymphoedema, typically Wuchereria bancrofti filariasis). (5.2) Complication: Recurrent secondary bacterial or fungal infections (recurrent acute dermatolymphangioadenitis / cellulitis, lymphorrhoea, ulceration, psychosocial disability).

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with exertional dyspnoea and a burning sensation on her tongue when eating, with the oral finding shown in the photograph. Her full blood count shows Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, and MCH 25 pg. Which confirmatory investigation profile best establishes the underlying cause?
options: Low serum ferritin with raised total iron-binding capacity
Elevated serum vitamin B12 with normal red cell folate
Raised reticulocyte count with positive direct Coombs test
Elevated HbA2 exceeding 3.5% on haemoglobin electrophoresis
High serum ferritin with reduced total iron-binding capacity
optionRationales: Correct: Atrophic glossitis with microcytic hypochromic anaemia (Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, MCH 25 pg) indicates iron deficiency anaemia, confirmed by low serum ferritin, low serum iron, and elevated TIBC—warranting evaluation for menorrhagia, occult GI blood loss, or hookworm.
Incorrect: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency produces macrocytic anaemia (MCV >100 fL) rather than microcytic hypochromic indices (MCV 70 fL).
Incorrect: A positive direct antiglobulin test and reticulocytosis confirm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, which is typically normocytic or mildly macrocytic.
Incorrect: Beta-thalassaemia trait elevates HbA2 but typically yields mild microcytosis with normal or minimally reduced haemoglobin (not symptomatic Hb 7.8 g/dL with glossitis).
Incorrect: Elevated ferritin with reduced TIBC reflects anaemia of chronic inflammation/disease rather than true iron depletion.
clinicalPearl: Always pair confirmation of iron deficiency anaemia (low serum ferritin) with identifying its cause: menorrhagia in premenopausal women, occult gastrointestinal malignancy in men and older adults, and hookworm infestation in endemic settings.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia (low MCV and MCH) with atrophic glossitis reflects iron deficiency, confirmed by low serum ferritin and followed up for blood loss.

sourceStation.title: Atrophic Glossitis & Iron Deficiency Anaemia
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1.1 A patient presented with burning sensations in her mouth while eating. Mention the clinical feature you can see in the picture.
1.2 Hb 7.8 g/dL | MCV 70 fL | MCH 25 pg. What could be the reason for these FBC findings?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1.1) Atrophic glossitis (smooth, depapillated tongue) ± angular cheilitis. (1.2) Reason for microcytic hypochromic anaemia: Iron deficiency anaemia (causes: chronic occult/GI blood loss, menorrhagia, hookworm infestation, nutritional deficiency; confirm with serum ferritin and GI/gynae evaluation).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 21-year-old man presents with 1 week of high fever and severe calf myalgia after bathing in a river. Physical examination demonstrates the ocular sign shown in the photograph alongside mild scleral icterus. Which life-threatening complications is he most specifically at risk of developing over the next several days?
options: Perforated duodenal ulcer and pneumoperitoneum
Ascending flaccid paralysis and bulbar palsy
Acute kidney injury and pulmonary haemorrhage
Acute retinal detachment and optic atrophy
Chronic constrictive pericarditis and tamponade
optionRationales: Incorrect: Peptic ulcer perforation presents with acute peritonism and subdiaphragmatic air rather than conjunctival suffusion and jaundiced febrile myalgia.
Incorrect: Ascending paralysis characterises Guillain-Barré syndrome or krait envenoming rather than acute leptospirosis.

Correct: Fever, calf myalgia, river/paddy water exposure, conjunctival suffusion (erythema without purulent exudate), and jaundice are diagnostic of severe leptospirosis (Weil's disease), which causes AKI, fulminant hepatic dysfunction, pulmonary haemorrhage, and myocarditis.
Incorrect: Severe leptospirosis may rarely cause late uveitis, whereas immediate mortality arises from pulmonary haemorrhage, acute renal failure, and myocarditis.
Incorrect: Leptospirosis causes acute myocarditis and arrhythmias rather than chronic fibrotic pericardial constriction.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan Medicine OSCEs, bilateral conjunctival suffusion (bright red conjunctival injection without pus) + calf tenderness + freshwater exposure = leptospirosis; monitor urine output, serum creatinine, platelets, and respiratory distress closely for Weil's syndrome and pulmonary haemorrhage.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Conjunctival suffusion with jaundice and river-water exposure indicates leptospirosis, risking acute kidney injury, pulmonary haemorrhage, myocarditis, and hepatitis.

sourceStation.title: Leptospirosis (Conjunctival Suffusion + Jaundice)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04) A 21-year-old male presented with a history of fever for 1 week and severe myalgia. He had recently bathed in a river.
1) What is the sign you see in the patient?
2) What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
3) List three (3) complications he could develop within a few days.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Conjunctival suffusion (with icterus). (2) Diagnosis: Leptospirosis (Weil's disease). (3) Complications: Acute kidney injury (AKI), Hepatic dysfunction/fulminant hepatitis, Pulmonary haemorrhage, Myocarditis / arrhythmias, Aseptic meningitis.

domainClean: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
topic: IV Cannula Selection for Blood Transfusion
stem: A 44-year-old man with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding requires an urgent packed red cell transfusion. Three peripheral intravenous cannulae (A, B, and C) are displayed on the ward trolley as shown in the photograph. Which cannula is standardly preferred for adult blood transfusion and why?
options: Cannula A (22G blue) to reduce the risk of transfusion-associated fluid overload
Cannula A (22G blue) because narrow bores minimise endothelial irritation
Cannula B (20G pink) because smaller lumens prevent platelet clumping
Cannula C (18G green) because it eliminates the need for blood warmers
Cannula C (18G green) to allow rapid flow without red cell haemolysis
optionRationales: Incorrect: Cannula A (22G blue) is too narrow for routine adult blood transfusion, impeding flow and increasing risk of mechanical haemolysis and clotting; fluid overload is prevented by infusion rate control and diuretics, not tiny cannulae.
Incorrect: While 22G blue cannulae suit maintenance fluids or fragile paediatric/elderly veins, they are unsuitable for urgent adult red cell resuscitation.
Incorrect: Although a 20G pink cannula can be used slowly in patients with very small veins, 18G green (C) is the standard preferred gauge for adult packed red cell transfusion.
Incorrect: Cannula gauge facilitates safe rapid flow without haemolysis, whereas blood warmers are still indicated during massive rapid transfusion to prevent hypothermia.
Correct: Cannula C is a wide-bore 18-gauge green cannula that permits rapid administration of viscous packed red blood cells with minimal mechanical shear haemolysis.
clinicalPearl: Know the CSS colour-code sequence from narrowest to widest: 24G Yellow -> 22G Blue (A) -> 20G Pink (B) -> 18G Green (C, standard blood transfusion) -> 16G Grey -> 14G Orange/Brown (massive trauma resuscitation).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Select an 18G green wide-bore IV cannula for standard adult packed red cell transfusion to enable brisk flow without shear haemolysis.

sourceStation.title: IV Cannula Selection for Blood Transfusion
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5) Three IV cannulae (A, B, C: blue, pink, green) are shown.
Select the cannula used for blood transfusions.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Green cannula (18G) — wide-bore cannula allows rapid flow of viscous packed red blood cells without haemolysis (20G Pink can be used in small veins/elderly if needed, but 18G Green is standard for adult transfusion).

domainClean: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency unit following a traumatic upper arm amputation. His pulse rate is 120 bpm, blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg, and he is anuric. Three intravenous fluid bottles (A, B, and C) are shown. Which pair correctly states his estimated blood volume loss and appropriate initial resuscitation fluid?
options: 15% to 30% blood loss; 5% dextrose (bottle A) to expand plasma volume
30% to 40% blood loss; 5% dextrose (bottle A) as rapid bolus
Less than 15% blood loss; isotonic crystalloid (bottle B or C) alone
Greater than 40% blood loss; 5% dextrose (bottle A) to prevent hypoglycaemia
Greater than 40% blood loss; isotonic crystalloid (bottle B or C) before blood
optionRationales: Incorrect: Class II haemorrhage (15–30%) maintains normal systolic blood pressure via tachycardia and vasoconstriction, and 5% dextrose rapidly equilibrates into intracellular water rather than expanding intravascular volume.
Incorrect: Anuria combined with 80/60 mmHg hypotension represents >40% loss (Class IV), and hypotonic 5% dextrose is contraindicated in shock resuscitation.
Incorrect: Class I haemorrhage (<15%) presents with normal heart rate, normal blood pressure, and preserved urine output.
Incorrect: Although blood loss exceeds 40%, 5% dextrose fails to restore circulating intravascular volume and risks cerebral/tissue oedema.

Correct: Marked tachycardia (120 bpm), severe hypotension (80/60 mmHg), and anuria define ATLS Class IV haemorrhagic shock (>40% blood volume loss), requiring immediate isotonic crystalloid resuscitation (Compound Sodium Lactate [B] or 0.9% NaCl [C]) while activating urgent cross-matched blood/massive transfusion.
clinicalPearl: Never pick 5% dextrose for hypovolaemic shock resuscitation: once dextrose is metabolised it behaves as free water; use isotonic crystalloid (Hartmann's/Compound Sodium Lactate or 0.9% NaCl) initially and transition urgently to blood in Class III/IV shock.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Class IV haemorrhage (>40% blood volume loss with hypotension, tachycardia, and anuria) requires initial isotonic crystalloid resuscitation and urgent blood transfusion.

sourceStation.title: Class IV Haemorrhagic Shock & Initial Fluid Resuscitation
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
7. A 30-year-old patient underwent a traumatic amputation of the upper arm. His pulse rate was 120 bpm and blood pressure was 80/60 mmHg. He was anuric. Three IV fluid bottles (A, B, C) are shown.
• Estimate the percentage of fluid loss due to haemorrhage.
• What is the most appropriate fluid for initial resuscitation?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Class IV Haemorrhage: above 40% blood volume loss (hypotension + tachycardia + anuria). (2) B — 0.9% Normal Saline (isotonic crystalloid; or Hartmann's/Ringer's lactate, followed urgently by cross-matched blood/massive transfusion protocol).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 27-year-old man previously treated by a native healer presents 6 days after a snakebite passing the dark brown urine shown in the photograph. Microscopy shows 1–2 red cells/hpf, 1–2 pus cells/hpf, no casts, negative bilirubin, and negative urobilinogen, while his haemoglobin falls from 13 g/dL to 6 g/dL in 24 hours. What explains the dark urine?
options: Gross glomerular haematuria from crescentic glomerulonephritis
Cholestatic obstructive jaundice with conjugated bilirubinuria
Haemoglobinuria secondary to acute intravascular haemolysis
Extravascular haemolysis causing excess urinary urobilinogen
Acute bacterial pyelonephritis with renal papillary necrosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: True glomerular haematuria shows abundant red cells and red cell casts on urine microscopy rather than 1–2 RBCs/hpf with no casts.
Incorrect: Obstructive jaundice produces positive urinary bilirubin rather than negative urinary bilirubin and an abrupt 7 g/dL drop in haemoglobin.

Correct: Dark cola-coloured urine with an acute 7 g/dL haemoglobin drop, virtually absent red cells on microscopy (1–2 RBC/hpf), and negative bilirubin/urobilinogen confirms free haemoglobinuria from acute intravascular haemolysis (triggered by viper venom or herbal nephro-haemotoxins).
Incorrect: Extravascular haemolysis elevates urinary urobilinogen (which is negative here) and does not spill free haemoglobin into the urine.
Incorrect: Pyelonephritis causes significant pyuria and bacteriuria rather than 1–2 pus cells/hpf with catastrophic acute anaemia.
clinicalPearl: Cola-coloured urine + positive dipstick blood + virtually NO red cells on microscopy = pigmenturia (haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria); aggressively hydrate with IV crystalloids and monitor renal function to prevent pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Viper envenoming or toxic herbal remedies can trigger acute intravascular haemolysis, presenting with steep Hb drop, dark urine, negative bilirubin, and minimal RBCs on microscopy.

sourceStation.title: Snakebite-Induced Intravascular Haemolysis (Haemoglobinuria)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. This is a urine sample of a 27-year-old male treated by a native physician for snakebite, 6 days after an alleged snakebite. Urine analysis:
Pus cells: 1–2/hpf | Red cells: 1–2/hpf | Casts: Nil | Bilirubin: Nil | Urobilinogen: Nil
His haemoglobin level dropped from 13 g/dL to 6 g/dL within one day.
What is the reason for dark-coloured urine?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Haemoglobinuria secondary to acute intravascular haemolysis (triggered by snake venom, e.g., Russell's viper / hump-nosed viper, or native herbal toxins; confirmed by cola/dark urine with positive dipstick blood but only 1–2 RBCs/hpf on microscopy and steep Hb drop).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 34-year-old farmer presents 12 hours after a snakebite on the dorsum of his foot with the haemorrhagic blister and local swelling shown in the photograph. Which pair of Sri Lankan snakes most characteristically produces this local bite-site appearance?
options: Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and Ceylon krait (Bungarus ceylonicus)
Hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale) and cobra (Naja naja)
Rat snake (Ptyas mucosa) and green vine snake (Ahaetulla nasuta)
Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus) and rat snake (Ptyas mucosa)
Beaked sea snake and Ceylon krait (Bungarus ceylonicus)
optionRationales: Incorrect: Kraits typically bite sleeping victims at night and produce descending neurotoxicity with minimal or absent local swelling, pain, or blistering.

Correct: Among these Sri Lankan species, hump-nosed vipers classically produce marked local swelling, haemorrhagic blistering, and necrosis (plus AKI/coagulopathy), and cobras similarly cause severe local blistering and tissue necrosis alongside neurotoxicity.
Incorrect: The rat snake is non-venomous and the mildly venomous vine snake does not cause severe haemorrhagic blistering or tissue necrosis.
Incorrect: Neither the non-venomous rat snake nor the krait produces severe haemorrhagic blisters at the bite site.
Incorrect: Sea snakes cause rhabdomyolysis/myotoxicity and neurotoxicity with minimal local bite-site inflammation, and kraits lack local necrotic blistering.
clinicalPearl: Remember the crucial Sri Lankan clinical rule: Indian polyvalent antivenom covers Cobra, Russell's viper, Common krait, and Saw-scaled viper—it is INEFFECTIVE against Hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale), which is managed supportively for local blistering, coagulopathy, and AKI.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Hump-nosed viper and cobra cause prominent local swelling and haemorrhagic blistering, whereas kraits cause severe neurotoxicity with minimal local signs.

sourceStation.title: Snakebite Local Envenoming (Haemorrhagic Blister)

Which of the following snake(s) is/are likely to have caused it? (Wrong answers carry minus marks):
• Cobra  • Hump-nosed viper  • Sri Lankan krait  • Indian krait  • Rat snake
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: *Hump-nosed viper (Hypnale hypnale) and/or Cobra (Naja naja) — both Sri Lankan species cause prominent local swelling, haemorrhagic blistering, and necrosis (Note: Kraits cause neurotoxicity with minimal/no local signs; Rat snake is non-venomous. Russell's viper also causes local blistering but wasn't listed; among the choices, Hump-nosed viper is classic for severe local haemorrhagic blisters/necrosis + AKI, and Cobra* causes local necrosis/blistering).

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: Two healthcare providers perform the resuscitation procedure shown in the photograph on an unresponsive adult with no carotid pulse and absent normal breathing. Which combination states the correct chest compression site, depth, and compression-to-ventilation ratio for adult Basic Life Support?
options: Lower half of sternum, 5–6 cm depth, 30:2 ratio
Upper half of sternum, 2–3 cm depth, 15:2 ratio
Lower half of sternum, 5–6 cm depth, 15:2 ratio
Left fifth intercostal space, 4 cm depth, 30:2 ratio
Tip of the xiphisternum, 3–4 cm depth, 5:1 ratio
optionRationales: Correct: Adult CPR with bag-valve-mask ventilation uses interlocked hands with straight arms over the lower half of the sternum, compressing 5–6 cm (about 2 inches) at 100–120/min in a 30 compressions to 2 breaths ratio.
Incorrect: Compressing the upper sternum at 2–3 cm fails to generate adequate intrathoracic cardiac output, and 15:2 applies to two-rescuer paediatric CPR rather than adults.
Incorrect: A 15:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio is used in two-rescuer paediatric resuscitation, whereas adult BLS uses 30:2 regardless of one or two rescuers prior to an advanced airway.
Incorrect: Compressions are delivered centrally over the lower half of the sternum, not laterally at the cardiac apex.
Incorrect: Pressing directly on the xiphisternum risks xiphoid fracture and hepatic laceration, and neither depth nor ratio meets adult BLS guidelines.
clinicalPearl: During two-rescuer BVM ventilation in an OSCE, hold the mask with an E-C clamp (thumb and index finger forming a C on the mask, remaining fingers lifting the mandible) and avoid hyperventilation—each breath should take 1 second just to produce visible chest rise.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Adult cardiac arrest CPR uses straight-arm compressions over the lower sternum to ~2 inches (5–6 cm) depth at a 30:2 ratio with BVM ventilation.

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department drowsy with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 5 breaths/min following an alleged heroin overdose. His ABG shows pH 7.25, PaO2 98 mmHg, PaCO2 60 mmHg, and HCO3- 30 mmol/L. Which interpretation and immediate management is most appropriate?
options: Metabolic acidosis; intravenous sodium bicarbonate and flumazenil
Compensated respiratory alkalosis; high-flow oxygen via face mask alone
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis; urgent haemodialysis and charcoal
Acute respiratory acidosis; assisted BVM ventilation and IV naloxone
Chronic respiratory acidosis; oral acetylcysteine and non-invasive ventilation
optionRationales: Incorrect: Bicarbonate is slightly elevated rather than low, proving respiratory acidosis; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines (and risks seizures) rather than opioids.
Incorrect: A low pH of 7.25 with high PaCO2 is acidosis, not alkalosis, and high-flow oxygen without ventilatory support or naloxone fails to clear life-threatening hypercapnia.
Incorrect: Activated charcoal is contraindicated in a drowsy patient without a secured airway, and heroin toxicity is reversed specifically by naloxone rather than dialysis.

Correct: Marked hypoventilation (RR 5/min) raises PaCO2 to 60 mmHg and drops pH to 7.25, representing acute respiratory acidosis from opioid toxicity; immediate management is airway/BVM ventilation with O2 plus titrated IV naloxone (monitoring closely for re-sedation as naloxone wears off faster than heroin).
Incorrect: The minimal bicarbonate rise relative to PaCO2 60 mmHg indicates acute hypoventilation, and acetylcysteine treats paracetamol poisoning rather than opioid overdose.
clinicalPearl: Never discharge or leave a heroin-overdose patient unmonitored after a single IV naloxone bolus: naloxone's half-life (30–60 min) is shorter than many opioids, so recurrent respiratory depression frequently develops.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Opioid-induced hypoventilation causes acute respiratory acidosis (low pH, high PaCO2); secure airway/BVM ventilation and administer titrated IV naloxone while watching for re-sedation.

sourceStation.title: Heroin Overdose — Acute Respiratory Acidosis & Management
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
18. A 20-year-old boy was admitted due to overdose of heroin. He was drowsy. Respiratory rate was 5/min. Arterial blood gas findings:
pH: 7.25 | PO2: 98 mmHg | PCO2: 60 mmHg | HCO3-: 30 mmol/L (24–29)
18.1 What is the abnormality in the blood gas findings?
18.2 What is the immediate management to correct the abnormality?  [Text-only ABG station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (18.1) Acute (uncompensated/partially compensated) respiratory acidosis due to opioid-induced central hypoventilation (low pH, markedly elevated PCO₂). (18.2) Immediate management: (a) Airway & breathing support (jaw thrust/airway adjunct, assisted BVM ventilation with O₂); (b) IV Naloxone (0.4–2 mg IV, titrated to restore adequate respiratory effort; monitor closely for re-sedation because naloxone half-life is shorter than heroin).

domain: 1.1 CARDIOLOGY & ECG INTERPRETATION (11 STATIONS)
topic: Acute Pericarditis vs STEMI ECG Differentiation
stem: A 29-year-old man presents with sharp central chest pain that worsens on deep inspiration and lying flat, and eases when leaning forward. His 12-lead ECG shows widespread upward-concave ST-segment elevation across precordial and limb leads without reciprocal ST depression. Which additional ECG feature strongly supports acute pericarditis over an acute myocardial infarction?
options: Diffuse PR-segment depression accompanied by PR-segment elevation in lead aVR
Deep symmetrical T-wave inversions with markedly prolonged QTc interval
Convex tombstone ST-segment elevation strictly confined to leads V1–V4
Tall broad R waves and horizontal ST-segment depression in leads V1–V2
Pathological Q waves in leads II, III, and aVF with ST depression in lead aVL
optionRationales: Correct: Per the ECG Reference Guide, acute pericarditis classically causes diffuse concave ST-segment elevation, no reciprocal ST depression, and PR-segment depression across most leads with reciprocal PR-segment elevation in lead aVR.
Incorrect: Deep symmetrical T-wave inversions with QTc prolongation (Wellens/ischaemic or Takotsubo pattern) point to myocardial ischaemia or stress cardiomyopathy rather than pericarditis.
Incorrect: Regional convex ST elevation confined to V1–V4 indicates acute anteroseptal STEMI rather than generalised pericardial inflammation.
Incorrect: Tall R waves with horizontal ST depression in V1–V2 represent acute posterior STEMI.
Incorrect: Inferior pathological Q waves with reciprocal ST depression in aVL reflect acute or established inferior myocardial infarction.
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya ECG Reference Guide, up to 43% of true STEMIs can show subtle concave STE early on—so always check for PR-segment depression, absence of reciprocal ST depression, and serial ECGs at 5–10 minute intervals when in doubt.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute pericarditis causes diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression (PR elevation in aVR), and no reciprocal ST depression.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
stem: A 54-year-old man who worked in an asbestos roofing-sheet factory for 18 years presents with progressively worsening exertional dyspnoea. Chest radiography demonstrates bilateral calcified pleural plaques and diaphragmatic calcifications, and HRCT reveals basal honeycombing. Which spirometric pattern and malignancy risk are characteristic of his condition?
options: Reduced FEV₁ and FVC with normal or elevated FEV₁/FVC ratio; malignant mesothelioma
Isolated reduction in peak expiratory flow with normal lung volumes; mediastinal thymoma
Reduced FEV₁ with normal FVC and FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70; small cell carcinoma
Increased total lung capacity with elevated DLCO; pulmonary chondroid hamartoma
Marked bronchodilator reversibility above 12% in FEV₁; bronchial carcinoid tumour
optionRationales: Correct: Per the CSS CXR Guide (Item 7), asbestosis causes restrictive lung physiology—reduction of both FEV₁ and FVC so the FEV₁/FVC ratio remains normal or >=70%—along with basal honeycombing, pleural/diaphragmatic calcifications, and high risk of malignant mesothelioma (as well as bronchogenic carcinoma).
Incorrect: Asbestosis reduces total lung volumes (TLC, FVC, FEV₁) and is linked to mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, not thymoma.
Incorrect: An FEV₁/FVC ratio <0.70 defines obstructive lung disease (such as COPD/asthma) rather than restrictive interstitial fibrosis.
Incorrect: Interstitial lung disease reduces total lung capacity and *lowers* (not elevates) DLCO, and hamartomas present as solitary nodules with 'popcorn' calcification.
Incorrect: Bronchodilator reversibility >12% and >200 mL characterises bronchial asthma rather than asbestos-related pulmonary fibrosis.
clinicalPearl: In Sri Lankan CXR OSCEs, remember the classic occupational pairing: asbestos sheet factory -> diaphragmatic calcifications + pleural plaques + lower-zone honeycombing + restrictive spirometry (FEV₁/FVC >=70%) + mesothelioma risk (whereas silicosis gives upper-zone fibrosis and 'eggshell' hilar nodes).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Asbestosis produces pleural/diaphragmatic calcifications, basal honeycombing, restrictive spirometry (FEV1/FVC >=70%), and mesothelioma risk.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Serial ABG Interpretation in Acute Asthma Exhaustion
stem: A 25-year-old woman with acute severe asthma arrives alert and tachypnoeic with an initial ABG showing pH 7.48, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, PaO₂ 68 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L. Despite nebulised bronchodilators and oxygen, a repeat ABG 1 hour later shows pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg, PaO₂ 80 mmHg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L, with reduced wheezing and drowsiness. How should this PaCO₂ trend be interpreted?
options: Onset of respiratory muscle exhaustion indicating life-threatening asthma requiring urgent ICU review
Inadvertent arterialisation of a venous sample with no change in ventilatory status
Renal compensation for acute hyperventilation confirming resolution of bronchospasm
Normalisation of ventilation confirming a favourable response to nebulised beta-2 agonist therapy
Primary metabolic alkalosis precipitated by repeated systemic corticosteroid administration
optionRationales: Correct: As highlighted in the CSS Blood Gas Analysis Guide, acutely breathless asthmatics initially hyperventilate and blow off CO₂ (PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, respiratory alkalosis). A rising PaCO₂ trend into the 'normal' or mildly elevated range (45 mmHg, pH 7.33) accompanied by a silent chest/drowsiness signifies respiratory muscle exhaustion and impending arrest.
Incorrect: Venous sampling does not explain clinical deterioration (drowsiness and reduced breath sounds/silent chest) alongside acute hypercapnic acidaemia.
Incorrect: Renal compensation lowers HCO₃⁻ slowly over days rather than elevating PaCO₂ over 1 hour.
Incorrect: Interpreting a 'normal' PaCO₂ of 45 mmHg in an exhausted asthmatic as reassuring improvement is a classic fatal error.
Incorrect: The pH has fallen from 7.48 to acidaemic 7.33 due to rising PaCO₂ (respiratory acidosis), not metabolic alkalosis.
clinicalPearl: Never be falsely reassured by a 'normal' PaCO₂ (35–45 mmHg) in an acute severe asthma attack—compare serial blood gases! A rising PaCO₂ + silent chest + exhaustion = life-threatening asthma requiring IV magnesium/aminophylline and urgent ICU/anaesthetic alert.

guideCitation.keyPoint: In acute severe asthma, a rising trend in PaCO2 (even into the 'normal' range) indicates ventilatory muscle exhaustion and life-threatening asthma.

domain: 1.4 ENDOCRINOLOGY & METABOLIC MEDICINE (12 STATIONS)
topic: High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis & ABG Analysis
stem: A 25-year-old woman is admitted drowsy after 3 days of polyuria, thirst, and dysuria. On room air, her ABG shows pH 7.20, PaCO₂ 24 mmHg, PaO₂ 100 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, and base excess −18 mmol/L; serum Na⁺ is 136 mmol/L, K⁺ 4.8 mmol/L, and Cl⁻ 100 mmol/L. Which acid-base disturbance is present, and what drives the anion gap?
options: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; renal bicarbonate wasting
Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation; sepsis-driven hyperventilation
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; accumulation of ketoacids
Mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis; alveolar hypoventilation with chloride retention
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis with normal anion gap; gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss
optionRationales: Incorrect: In normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) acidosis, serum chloride rises proportionally as HCO₃⁻ falls so the anion gap remains normal (~10–14 mmol/L with K⁺), unlike the markedly elevated gap here.
Incorrect: The arterial pH is severely acidaemic (7.20), whereas primary respiratory alkalosis produces alkalaemia (pH >7.45).

Correct: A low pH (7.20), low HCO₃⁻ (10 mmol/L), and markedly negative base excess (−18 mmol/L) define primary metabolic acidosis; PaCO₂ has fallen appropriately to 24 mmHg via Kussmaul hyperventilation (Winter's formula: 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 mmHg), and the anion gap (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) = 30.8 mmol/L is elevated by unmeasured ketoacids in DKA.
Incorrect: PaCO₂ is appropriately suppressed to 24 mmHg (hyperventilation), ruling out concomitant respiratory acidosis.
Incorrect: Compensatory hyperventilation has lowered PaCO₂ to 24 mmHg, and the calculated anion gap is substantially elevated rather than normal.
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya ABG Guide, base excess and standard HCO₃⁻ quantify the metabolic component independently of acute PaCO₂ changes, while the anion gap (Na⁺ + K⁺) − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) separates keto/lactic acidosis from hyperchloraemic diarrhoea/RTA.

guideCitation.keyPoint: High anion gap metabolic acidosis reduces HCO3- via addition of unmeasured anions (e.g. ketoacids, lactate), whereas normal anion gap acidosis raises Cl-.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Glasgow Coma Scale Scoring & Head Injury Severity
stem: A 42-year-old motorcyclist is brought to the Emergency Treatment Unit after a road traffic collision. On examination, he opens his eyes only to firm nail-bed pressure, produces incomprehensible groaning sounds without intelligible words, and demonstrates abnormal slow flexion of both elbows across his chest to painful stimulation. What is his total GCS score and head injury classification?
options: GCS 7/15 (E1 V3 M3); moderate head injury
GCS 7/15 (E2 V2 M3); severe head injury
GCS 9/15 (E3 V2 M4); moderate head injury
GCS 8/15 (E2 V2 M4); severe head injury
GCS 6/15 (E2 V2 M2); severe head injury
optionRationales: Incorrect: E1 is no eye opening at all and V3 is inappropriate words; furthermore, a total GCS of 7 is classified as severe (<=8), not moderate (9–12).

Correct: Per the CSS GCS Guide, eye opening to peripheral pain scores E2, incomprehensible sounds score V2, and abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) scores M3, giving a total of 7/15; a GCS of 8 or less defines coma and severe head injury.
Incorrect: E3 represents eye opening to verbal command rather than to pain (E2), and M4 represents withdrawal rather than abnormal flexion.
Incorrect: M4 represents normal purposeful withdrawal away from a painful stimulus rather than stereotyped abnormal decorticate flexion (M3).
Incorrect: M2 represents abnormal extension (decerebrate posturing), whereas slow flexion of the elbows across the chest is M3.
clinicalPearl: Key rules from the Kelaniya GCS OSCE Guide: never apply painful stimuli to the face when testing eye opening (use trapezius pinch or nail-bed pressure), record the best motor response across limbs, and remember 'GCS <= 8 = coma / severe head injury — consider intubation'.

guideCitation.keyPoint: GCS classification: Severe <=8 (Coma), Moderate 9–12, Mild 13–15; abnormal flexion (decorticate) = M3 and eye opening to non-facial pain = E2.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Metered-Dose Inhaler & Spacer Device Technique and Care
stem: A 46-year-old man with moderate persistent asthma is prescribed a beclomethasone dipropionate metered-dose inhaler (MDI) used with a large-volume plastic spacer. Which instruction regarding inhaler use and spacer maintenance is essential to maximise lung deposition and prevent local side effects?
options: Inhale as fast and forcefully as possible as soon as the MDI canister is depressed into the spacer
Actuate two puffs together into the spacer chamber before taking one deep breath-hold
Place the disassembled spacer halves in direct midday sunlight weekly for rapid thermal sterilisation
Wipe the inside of the plastic chamber dry with a clean cloth after washing to clear static droplets
Clean with lukewarm water, air-dry in the shade without wiping the inside, and rinse mouth after use
optionRationales: Incorrect: Fast, forceful inhalation is required for dry powder inhalers (DPIs) to de-aggregate powder; an MDI/spacer requires a slow, steady, deep inhalation followed by a 10-second breath-hold.
Incorrect: Actuating multiple puffs into a spacer simultaneously causes aerosol collision and rain-out inside the chamber, markedly reducing the delivered dose; always administer one puff at a time.
Incorrect: Drying a spacer in direct sunlight warps plastic components and degrades valve integrity; always air-dry in a shaded, ventilated area.

Incorrect: Rubbing or towel-drying the interior of a plastic spacer damages its antistatic property and creates static charge that attracts drug particles onto the walls instead of reaching the lungs.

Correct: Per the CSS Inhalers & Spacer Guide, washing the spacer every 2 weeks in lukewarm water (with mild detergent) and air-drying in the shade without rubbing the interior preserves its antistatic lining, while rinsing and gargling after steroid inhalation prevents oral candidiasis and dysphonia.
clinicalPearl: High-yield CSS spacer viva points: spacers evaporate propellant to reduce particle size and trap large particles—slashing oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia—provided you actuate 1 puff at a time and never rub the inside dry.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Wash plastic spacers in lukewarm water and air-dry in the shade without rubbing inside (preserves antistatic lining); actuate 1 puff at a time and rinse mouth after ICS.

domain: 1.2 RESPIRATORY MEDICINE, CHEST IMAGING & AIRWAY EQUIPMENT (14 STATIONS)
topic: Blood Gas Analysis — PaO2/FiO2 Ratio & Inspired Oxygen
stem: A 35-year-old man admitted with dyspnoea following a stab injury to the chest has an arterial blood gas showing pH 7.48, PaO2 90 mmHg, and PaCO2 32 mmHg. Which additional parameter is essential to interpret this PaO2 value and accurately quantify impaired oxygenation?
options: Serum haemoglobin concentration to calculate total arterial oxygen content
Inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2) to calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio
Standard bicarbonate level to evaluate acute respiratory alkalosis compensation
Central venous oxygen saturation to determine tissue oxygen extraction
Alveolar minute ventilation to assess carbon dioxide clearance capacity
optionRationales: Incorrect: Although haemoglobin determines total blood oxygen-carrying capacity, PaO2 reflects dissolved plasma oxygen tension driven by alveolar-capillary transfer relative to inspired FiO2, not haemoglobin concentration.

Correct: Arterial PaO2 cannot be interpreted in isolation; dividing PaO2 by FiO2 (for example, PaO2 90 mmHg on FiO2 0.50 yields a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180 mmHg, compared with 450 mmHg on room air) is essential to quantify gas-exchange impairment and shunt.

Incorrect: Standard bicarbonate evaluates the non-respiratory (metabolic) acid-base component (which explains his mild alkalotic pH 7.48 from hyperventilation to PaCO2 32 mmHg), rather than quantifying pulmonary oxygenation.
Incorrect: Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) from a VBG assesses global systemic oxygen supply-to-demand balance rather than quantifying alveolar oxygenation efficiency on an ABG.
Incorrect: Minute ventilation governs PaCO2 elimination (ventilation), whereas quantifying impaired oxygen transfer requires relating arterial PaO2 to the inspired oxygen fraction (FiO2).
clinicalPearl: Per the Kelaniya Blood Gas Analysis guide, never label a PaO2 of 90–100 mmHg as normal without checking FiO2: calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio (normal >400 mmHg; <=300 mmHg indicates impaired gas exchange) and recognise that PaO2 90 mmHg on FiO2 0.50 equals a P/F ratio of 180 mmHg.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Quantifying oxygenation on an ABG requires factoring in inspired FiO2 (via the PaO2/FiO2 ratio) rather than interpreting PaO2 in isolation.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Ulnar Paradox in Peripheral Nerve Palsies
stem: A 28-year-old woman sustains a deep laceration across the medial anterior wrist, developing marked clawing of the ring and little fingers with MCP hyperextension and IP flexion. Compared with a complete ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow, why is the claw-hand deformity more pronounced in this distal wrist injury?
options: The extensor digitorum communis and extensor indicis are denervated at the wrist
All four lumbrical muscles are spared when the nerve is cut proximal to Guyon's canal
The palmar interossei receive dual innervation from the anterior interosseous nerve
The flexor carpi ulnaris pulls the proximal phalanges into hyperextension
The medial half of flexor digitorum profundus remains intact to flex the DIP joints
optionRationales: Incorrect: Digital extensors are innervated proximally in the forearm by the posterior interosseous branch of the radial nerve, not the ulnar nerve at the wrist.
Incorrect: The ulnar nerve supplies the third and fourth lumbricals distally in the hand, so they are paralysed in both wrist and elbow lesions.
Incorrect: All palmar and dorsal interossei are innervated exclusively by the deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve.
Incorrect: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts onto the pisiform/fifth metacarpal base to flex and adduct the wrist, without extending the MCP joints.

Correct: In the 'ulnar paradox', a wrist lesion spares the proximal ulnar branches in the forearm to the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP), so unopposed FDP pulls the interphalangeal joints into exaggerated flexion when the medial lumbricals are paralysed.
clinicalPearl: Always remember the 'ulnar paradox' in Neurology OSCE stations: distal ulnar nerve lesions at the wrist produce uglier, more severe clawing of digits 4–5 than proximal lesions at the elbow because FDP remains intact.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Ulnar paradox: a wrist lesion causes worse clawing than an elbow lesion because proximal innervation to the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus is preserved.

domain: 1.3 NEUROLOGY, CRANIAL NERVES & NEUROMUSCULAR DISORDERS (14 STATIONS)
topic: Retina & Fundoscopy — Central Retinal Vein Occlusion
stem: A 64-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension and primary open-angle glaucoma develops sudden, painless unilateral visual loss in his right eye. Direct ophthalmoscopy reveals disc hyperaemia, markedly engorged tortuous retinal veins, and widespread haemorrhages radiating across all four quadrants ('stormy sunset' appearance). What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Central retinal vein occlusion
Central retinal artery occlusion
Proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Primary glaucomatous optic atrophy
Dry age-related macular degeneration
optionRationales: Correct: Sudden painless visual loss with severely engorged tortuous veins and diffuse four-quadrant retinal haemorrhages ('stormy sunset' fundus) is the textbook presentation of central retinal vein occlusion, classically linked with hypertension and glaucoma.

Incorrect: Central retinal artery occlusion produces a pale, ischaemic retina with attenuated arteries and a central 'cherry-red spot' at the fovea rather than diffuse four-quadrant venous haemorrhages.

Incorrect: Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is characterised by fragile new vessel formation (neovascularisation at the disc or elsewhere) rather than acute unilateral four-quadrant venous engorgement.
Incorrect: Advanced glaucoma produces gradual peripheral field loss with a pale, widened, deeply excavated optic cup rather than sudden haemorrhagic engorgement.
Incorrect: Dry macular degeneration causes gradual central visual distortion with choroidal drusen and macular pigment changes rather than acute diffuse retinal haemorrhages.
clinicalPearl: Know the iconic Kelaniya Retina OSCE spotter descriptors: CRVO = 'stormy sunset' engorged veins and haemorrhages; malignant hypertensive retinopathy = 'star-burst' macular exudates + papilloedema; CRAO = pale retina + cherry-red spot.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Central retinal vein occlusion shows a 'stormy sunset' fundus with engorged tortuous veins and extensive accompanying retinal haemorrhages.

domain: 1.6 DERMATOLOGY, RHEUMATOLOGY, HAEMATOLOGY & INFECTIONS (15 STATIONS)
stem: A 44-year-old man with obesity presents with asymptomatic, well-demarcated reddish-brown scaly plaques in both groins and axillae. A fungal scraping for hyphae is negative, and Wood's ultraviolet light examination demonstrates bright coral-red fluorescence. Which organism is responsible for this infection?
options: Trichophyton rubrum
Malassezia furfur
Candida albicans
Corynebacterium minutissimum
Streptococcus pyogenes
optionRationales: Incorrect: Tinea cruris due to Trichophyton rubrum shows branching hyphae on KOH microscopy, an active raised scaly border with central clearing, and no coral-red Wood's light fluorescence.
Incorrect: Pityriasis versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur affects the upper trunk and exhibits pale yellow-green fluorescence under Wood's light rather than coral-red flexural plaques.
Incorrect: Candidal intertrigo produces bright beefy-red macerated plaques with satellite pustules and does not fluoresce coral-red on Wood's lamp examination.

Correct: Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin-fold infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum; bacterial coproporphyrin III production causes characteristic coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp.
Incorrect: Erysipelas due to beta-haemolytic streptococci causes acute painful, febrile, raised erythematous plaques rather than indolent brown scaly plaques with porphyrin fluorescence.
clinicalPearl: In the Kelaniya Bone & Skin Infections guide, differentiate groin/axillary plaques rapidly using Wood's light: coral-red fluorescence confirms Corynebacterium minutissimum erythrasma (treated with topical/oral erythromycin or fusidic acid) rather than tinea.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Erythrasma (Corynebacterium minutissimum) forms well-defined reddish-brown flexural plaques exhibiting coral-red Wood's lamp fluorescence from porphyrins.

domain: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT (8 STATIONS)
stem: A 32-year-old paddy farmer is bitten on the right ankle by a viper while working in the field and arrives at a rural clinic 15 minutes later. Which immediate pre-hospital first-aid action is recommended by the Emergency Medicine OSCE protocol prior to urgent hospital transfer?
options: Apply a tight proximal arterial tourniquet above the right knee
Make shallow cruciform incisions over the fang marks to drain venom
Remove tight ornaments, immobilise the limb, and transfer urgently
Pack the bitten foot in crushed ice to slow systemic venom spread
Administer intramuscular adrenaline prophylactically before transfer
optionRationales: Incorrect: Arterial tourniquets are strictly contraindicated because they exacerbate local ischaemic necrosis and can precipitate sudden systemic venom bolus release upon removal.
Incorrect: Incising or sucking the bite wound is ineffective and risks severe bleeding in viper-induced coagulopathy alongside secondary wound infection.

Correct: Emergency Medicine CSS protocol mandates removing rings, anklets, and tight clothing (before swelling progresses), gently cleansing with soap and water if soiled, immobilising the bitten limb, and transferring to hospital ASAP.
Incorrect: Cryotherapy with ice packs worsens local tissue ischaemia and necrosis without reducing systemic envenoming.
Incorrect: Adrenaline is reserved for treating acute anaphylaxis (for example, reactions to antivenom) rather than routine initial snakebite first aid.
clinicalPearl: Kelaniya Emergency Medicine OSCE 'Should Do / Should Not Do' checklist for snakebites: DO remove ornaments, reassure, immobilise, and get to hospital ASAP; DO NOT apply tourniquets or make incisions.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Immediate snakebite first aid: remove tight ornaments, cleanse gently, immobilise the limb, and transfer to hospital ASAP; never apply tourniquets or incise the wound.

domainClean: 1.7 TOXICOLOGY, SNAKEBITE, ACUTE CARE & CLINICAL EQUIPMENT

domain: 1.5 GASTROENTEROLOGY, HEPATOLOGY, RENAL & FLUID/ACID-BASE (7 STATIONS)
stem: A 35-year-old man with acute watery diarrhoea and mild dehydration is prescribed WHO reduced-osmolarity Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS), prepared by dissolving one 20.5 g packet in 1 litre of clean drinking water. Which statement accurately describes its osmolarity and physiological action?
options: Total osmolarity is 311 mmol/L; hypertonic glucose draws water passively into the gut lumen
Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L; sodium bicarbonate prevents hypokalaemic paralytic ileus
Total osmolarity is 150 mmol/L; potassium chloride directly neutralises bacterial enterotoxins
Total osmolarity is 330 mmol/L; active chloride secretion drives intestinal water absorption
Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L; Na+-glucose co-transport stays intact and citrate corrects acidosis
optionRationales: Incorrect: The older 311 mmol/L formulation was replaced by 245 mmol/L ORS precisely to reduce osmotic diarrhoea, and water follows sodium-glucose absorption out of the lumen into enterocytes.
Incorrect: Modern WHO ORS uses trisodium citrate dihydrate (rather than bicarbonate, for longer shelf stability) to treat acidosis, while potassium chloride prevents hypokalaemic ileus.
Incorrect: Total osmolarity is 245 mmol/L (not 150 mmol/L), and potassium chloride replaces faecal potassium losses rather than neutralising toxins.
Incorrect: Active chloride secretion (as triggered by cholera toxin via cAMP) causes secretory fluid loss; ORS works via intact glucose-coupled sodium absorption.

Correct: WHO reduced-osmolarity ORS (245 mmol/L: Na+ 75, glucose 75, Cl- 65, K+ 20, citrate 10 mmol/L) relies on coupled Na+-glucose co-transport (SGLT1), which remains intact even during enteritis, while KCl prevents hypokalaemia and trisodium citrate corrects metabolic acidosis.
clinicalPearl: Know the exact Kelaniya ORS OSCE numbers: 1 packet (20.5 g) in 1 L clean drinking water gives 245 mmol/L (Na+ 75, glucose 75, K+ 20, Cl- 65, citrate 10 mmol/L); discard unused solution after 24 hours, and switch to IV fluids if altered mental status, ileus, or persistent vomiting prevents oral intake.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Reduced-osmolarity WHO ORS (245 mmol/L; 20.5 g/L) exploits intact Na+-glucose co-transport, provides K+ (20 mmol/L) against hypokalaemia, and uses trisodium citrate (10 mmol/L) to correct acidosis.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 52-year-old man with chronic knee osteoarthritis taking daily non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs presents with sudden-onset, severe generalised abdominal pain and board-like rigidity. An erect chest radiograph demonstrates a crescentic lucency beneath the right hemidiaphragm. What is the most likely underlying surgical cause of this radiological finding?
options: Acute uncomplicated gallstone biliary colic
Perforated peptic ulcer (duodenal or gastric)
Acute interstitial oedematous pancreatitis
Simple adhesive small bowel obstruction
Right-sided subpulmonic pleural effusion
optionRationales: Incorrect: Uncomplicated biliary colic causes episodic right upper quadrant pain without visceral perforation or free intraperitoneal gas.
Correct: Subdiaphragmatic free gas (pneumoperitoneum) on an erect chest radiograph is most commonly caused by a perforated duodenal or gastric ulcer, strongly linked to chronic NSAID use.
Incorrect: Acute pancreatitis typically causes epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised amylase, occasionally producing a sentinel loop rather than free subdiaphragmatic air.
Incorrect: Simple small bowel obstruction produces dilated loops and multiple air-fluid levels on abdominal X-ray, not free subphrenic gas unless complicated by perforation.
Incorrect: A subpulmonic pleural effusion causes apparent elevation of the hemidiaphragm above the lung base rather than a crescentic gas lucency beneath the diaphragm.
clinicalPearl: An erect chest X-ray is the most sensitive plain radiograph for detecting pneumoperitoneum (as little as 1–2 mL of free gas); perforated peptic ulcer is the commonest cause.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Crescentic lucency under the right hemidiaphragm represents pneumoperitoneum, classically caused by a perforated peptic ulcer.

sourceStation.title: Pneumoperitoneum (Right Subdiaphragmatic Air)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
03. Photograph of an erect chest X-ray (right-sided subdiaphragmatic air collection marked by arrow).
What is the abnormality shown by the arrow, and most possible cause?  [CXR omitted in text-only 2012 archive PDF]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Right-sided subdiaphragmatic air collection (pneumoperitoneum). Causes: Perforated duodenal/peptic ulcer (most common), Perforated diverticulum, Bowel malignancy perforation, Necrotising enterocolitis, Penetrating abdominal trauma, Subdiaphragmatic gas-forming abscess.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 66-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of severe colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, progressive abdominal bloating, and failure to pass flatus or stool. Her plain abdominal radiograph is shown. After initial intravenous resuscitation and nasogastric decompression, which imaging modality is most definitive for confirming the transition point, identifying the underlying cause, and assessing for bowel ischaemia?
options: Oral barium follow-through meal study
Transabdominal pelvic ultrasonography alone
Flexible sigmoidoscopy without insufflation
Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Tc-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy scan
optionRationales: Incorrect: Oral barium is contraindicated in suspected acute complete or strangulated bowel obstruction due to risks of inspissation and barium peritonitis if perforation occurs.
Incorrect: Abdominal ultrasound is limited by overlying bowel gas in acute obstruction and cannot reliably delineate deep transition points across the entire bowel.
Incorrect: Endoscopy carries perforation risk in acute obstruction and does not evaluate extraluminal causes such as adhesions or closed-loop small bowel ischaemia.

Correct: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the gold standard after initial plain radiography to confirm mechanical bowel obstruction, locate the transition point, determine the cause (e.g., adhesions, hernia, tumour), and detect strangulation.
Incorrect: Tc-99m pertechnetate scanning detects ectopic gastric mucosa in Meckel's diverticulum rather than acute adult mechanical intestinal obstruction.
clinicalPearl: Plain erect and supine abdominal X-rays screen for dilated loops and air-fluid levels, whereas contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis defines the exact transition point, cause (adhesions, hernia, tumour, volvulus), and ischaemia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Initial obstruction care includes NBM, IV fluids, and Ryle's tube decompression, followed by contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis to pinpoint the transition site and exclude strangulation.

sourceStation.title: Intestinal Obstruction
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05. A 66-year-old female presents with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, bloating, and not passing gas or stool for 2 days.
What is the diagnosis? How do you investigate to confirm the diagnosis? Give 3 reasons for this happening.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Bowel (intestinal) obstruction. Investigations: Erect & supine Abdominal X-ray (dilated bowel loops with multiple air-fluid levels), Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis (transition point & cause), Ultrasound / Endoscopy (once stabilised/selected). Causes: Strangulated hernia, Colorectal carcinoma, Adhesions, Volvulus (sigmoid/caecal), Faecal impaction, Ascaris lumbricoides bolus.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 48-year-old man presents to the casualty unit with sudden epigastric pain and generalised abdominal guarding. An erect chest radiograph is obtained as shown. What is the principal radiological diagnosis?
options: Bilateral basal subpulmonic pleural effusions
Right-sided Chilaiditi colonic interposition
Bilateral subphrenic free air (pneumoperitoneum)
Bilateral apical tension pneumothoraces
Bilateral lower-lobe bullous emphysema
optionRationales: Incorrect: Subpulmonic effusions appear as homogeneous fluid opacity flattening and mimicking a high hemidiaphragm rather than sharp crescentic air lucencies beneath both domes.
Incorrect: Chilaiditi sign is asymptomatic colonic interposition beneath the right hemidiaphragm only, identifiable by visible colonic haustral markings rather than smooth bilateral free gas.

Correct: Smooth crescentic air lucencies beneath both the right and left hemidiaphragms (distinct from the gastric bubble below the left dome) confirm bilateral subphrenic pneumoperitoneum from hollow viscus perforation.
Incorrect: Pneumothorax demonstrates air within the pleural space outlining a retracted visceral pleural edge without peripheral lung markings, rather than subdiaphragmatic gas.
Incorrect: Bullous emphysema produces thin-walled parenchymal air spaces above the diaphragm within the lung fields rather than crescentic subphrenic collections.
clinicalPearl: Always check beneath both hemidiaphragms on an erect chest X-ray: free subphrenic gas appears as a crisp crescent outlining the diaphragm's inferior border, unlike haustrated bowel in Chilaiditi sign.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Gas under both hemidiaphragms indicates bilateral pneumoperitoneum from hollow viscus perforation and must be differentiated from hepatodiaphragmatic colonic interposition (Chilaiditi sign).

sourceStation.title: Bilateral Subphrenic Air Collection
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01)
a) What is the radiological diagnosis?
b) Causes for that.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Bilateral subphrenic air collection (pneumoperitoneum). (b) Causes: Perforated duodenal/peptic ulcer (most common), Ruptured appendix, Perforated diverticulum, Bowel obstruction with perforation, Bowel cancer, Penetrating trauma, Toxic megacolon.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 65-year-old man presents with altered bowel habits, fresh per-rectal bleeding, and tenesmus. Colonoscopy demonstrates the ulcerated lesion shown at the rectosigmoid junction, and biopsy confirms the commonest malignant histological subtype. Which combination of imaging studies is specifically required next for complete local and distant staging prior to definitive surgical planning?
options: Contrast CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with pelvic MRI
Erect chest radiograph and supine abdominal radiograph alone
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and MRCP
Double-contrast barium enema and Meckel's radioisotope scan
Ultrasound KUB with technetium-99m bone scintigraphy
optionRationales: Correct: Colorectal adenocarcinoma (accounting for >95% of cases) requires contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis for nodal/liver/lung staging plus MRI pelvis to define local rectal/mesorectal fascia invasion.
Incorrect: Plain radiographs cannot stage hepatic metastases, regional lymphadenopathy, or circumferential resection margin involvement.
Incorrect: ERCP and MRCP evaluate the biliary tree and pancreatic duct rather than local or distant staging of rectosigmoid carcinoma.
Incorrect: Barium enema offers only luminal contour imaging without nodal or distant staging, and Meckel's scanning is irrelevant to colorectal neoplasia.
Incorrect: Ultrasound KUB and bone scans do not evaluate mesorectal tumour depth or pulmonary and hepatic parenchymal metastases adequately.
clinicalPearl: Colorectal adenocarcinoma staging combines CECT chest/abdomen/pelvis (distant liver/lung metastases) with pelvic MRI (local T-stage and mesorectal margin) plus baseline serum CEA for post-operative surveillance.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Preoperative staging of colorectal adenocarcinoma includes CECT chest/abdomen/pelvis and pelvic MRI alongside baseline CEA to guide surgery and post-operative recurrence monitoring.

sourceStation.title: Rectosigmoid Adenocarcinoma (Colonoscopy)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01) 65-year-old male undergoing a colonoscopy shows the following appearance at the rectosigmoid junction.
1) List three (3) symptoms you will see in this patient.
2) What is the most probable histological diagnosis?
3) List two specific investigations that you should do to decide on further management.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Symptoms: Altered bowel habits (new-onset constipation/diarrhoea), Fresh per-rectal bleeding / blood mixed with stool, Tenesmus / feeling of incomplete evacuation, Unexplained weight loss / iron-deficiency anaemia. (2) Histology: Adenocarcinoma (colorectal adenocarcinoma). (3) Investigations: Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) chest, abdomen & pelvis (distant/nodal staging) and MRI pelvis (local rectal/mesorectal staging) ± serum CEA baseline and endoscopic biopsy.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 59-year-old man presents with acute peritonitis and hypotension; his erect chest radiograph is shown. Which pair of surgical pathologies represents the commonest non-traumatic causes of this radiological appearance?
options: Acute uncomplicated cholecystitis and ureteric colic
Adhesive small bowel obstruction and paralytic ileus
Acute oedematous pancreatitis and mesenteric adenitis
Intramural duodenal haematoma and splenic infarction
Perforated peptic ulcer and perforated colon carcinoma
optionRationales: Incorrect: Uncomplicated biliary and ureteric stone disease do not breach the gastrointestinal lumen to release free intraperitoneal air.
Incorrect: Simple mechanical obstruction or adynamic ileus distends intraluminal bowel gas without producing free subdiaphragmatic air unless perforation supervenes.
Incorrect: Acute oedematous pancreatitis and mesenteric adenitis cause retroperitoneal or peritoneal inflammation without hollow viscus perforation.
Incorrect: Intramural haematoma and splenic infarction remain confined to organ parenchyma or bowel wall without releasing intraluminal gas into the peritoneal cavity.

Correct: Free air under the diaphragm reflects gastrointestinal perforation, most frequently due to a perforated peptic (duodenal/gastric) ulcer or perforated colonic pathology (carcinoma, diverticulitis, or ruptured appendix).
clinicalPearl: Pneumoperitoneum in a patient with peritonism signals a surgical emergency—perforated peptic ulcer and colonic perforation (malignancy/diverticulitis) top the differential.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Free subdiaphragmatic gas signifies hollow viscus perforation, chiefly from perforated peptic ulcer disease or perforated colonic malignancy/diverticulitis.

sourceStation.title: Pneumoperitoneum on Erect CXR
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2)
• What is the diagnosis?
• Write 2 causes.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum). Causes: Perforated peptic (duodenal/gastric) ulcer, Bowel perforation (malignancy, diverticulitis, ruptured appendix), Trauma.

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: A 42-year-old man with chronic constipation presents to casualty with severe, unremitting anal pain and an irreducible, tense, dark-purple perianal mass with surface bleeding for 24 hours, as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis and the definitive surgical procedure indicated if severe pain or impending necrosis persists within 48–72 hours?
options: Intersphincteric perianal abscess; loop colostomy formation
Full-thickness rectal prolapse; laparoscopic ventral rectopexy
Thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoid; urgent haemorrhoidectomy
Chronic posterior anal fissure; botulinum toxin injection
Perianal squamous carcinoma; inguinal lymph node dissection
optionRationales: Incorrect: An abscess presents as a fluctuant, erythematous perianal swelling requiring simple incision and drainage rather than faecal diversion.
Incorrect: Full-thickness rectal prolapse shows concentric mucosal rings rather than an isolated engorged, thrombosed vascular cushion.

Correct: A tense, irreducible, purplish haemorrhoidal mass indicates an acute thrombosed/strangulated prolapsed haemorrhoid; within 48–72 hours of severe pain or gangrene, urgent surgical haemorrhoidectomy provides definitive relief.
Incorrect: Anal fissures present with tearing pain on defaecation and a sentinel skin tag rather than a large irreducible dark congested vascular mass.
Incorrect: Perianal squamous cell carcinoma develops slowly as an indurated ulcerating plaque rather than an acute 24-hour painful thrombosed swelling.
clinicalPearl: Acute thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids presenting within 48–72 hours with severe pain or necrosis benefit from urgent haemorrhoidectomy; late (>72 h) resolving cases are managed conservatively with analgesia, sitz baths, and stool softeners.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Acute thrombosed prolapsed haemorrhoids require pain control and stool softeners, with urgent haemorrhoidectomy reserved for severe pain or strangulation within 48–72 hours.

sourceStation.title: Prolapsed Thrombosed Haemorrhoid
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
09.
9.1 What is the most likely cause?
9.2 What is the most appropriate next step in the management?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (9.1) Thrombosed / strangulated prolapsed internal (or external) haemorrhoid. (9.2) Management: Analgesia, stool softeners, ice packs/warm sitz baths, and rest; if presenting acutely within 48–72 hours with severe pain/gangrene, perform urgent surgical haemorrhoidectomy (or clot evacuation under local anaesthesia for external thrombosed perianal haematoma).

domain: 2.1 GASTROINTESTINAL, HEPATOBILIARY & ACUTE ABDOMEN (13 STATIONS)
stem: An 18-year-old male undergoing diagnostic laparoscopy for left upper quadrant pain is found to have gross splenomegaly with surface nodularity and cystic changes, as shown. Which pair of peripheral blood smear findings would specifically reflect chronic haemolytic disease or functional hyposplenism in this patient?
options: Auer rods and circulating myeloblasts
Howell-Jolly bodies and erythrocyte target cells
Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes
Smudge cells and mature lymphocytosis
Rouleaux formation and circulating plasma cells
optionRationales: Incorrect: Auer rods inside myeloblasts are pathognomonic for acute myeloid leukaemia rather than functional hyposplenism or haemolytic anaemia.

Correct: Target cells (seen in thalassaemia/haemoglobinopathies causing splenomegaly) and Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants cleared by a functioning spleen) classically appear on the blood film in haemolytic/hyposplenic states.
Incorrect: Hypersegmented neutrophils and macro-ovalocytes are characteristic of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia).
Incorrect: Smudge (basket) cells with mature lymphocytosis are typical of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia.
