domain: 3.2 INTRAPARTUM CARE: PARTOGRAM & LABOUR ABNORMALITIES (6 STATIONS)
stem: A woman's active-phase cervical dilatation is plotted on the partograph shown. If her plotted dilatation curve moves to the right of the first diagonal line and subsequently crosses the second parallel diagonal line 4 hours later, which clinical labour pattern and management principle apply?
options: Normal physiological active-phase labour progressing at ≥ 1 cm/hour
Precipitate labour with cervical dilatation exceeding 5 cm/hour
Prolonged latent phase prior to entering active labour at 4 cm
Prolonged or abnormal labour requiring urgent senior reassessment of the 3 Ps
Normal passive phase of the second stage before maternal expulsive effort
optionRationales: Incorrect: Normal active labour progresses at ≥1 cm/hour, keeping the dilatation curve on or to the left of the Alert line.
Incorrect: Precipitate labour is abnormally rapid delivery (<3 hours total), which moves steeply to the left of the Alert line.
Incorrect: Both diagonal lines begin at 4 cm in the active phase; crossing them reflects active-phase delay rather than latent-phase prolongation.

Correct: Crossing the Alert line signals slow active-phase progress (<1 cm/hr), and crossing the Action line 4 hours later confirms abnormal/prolonged labour mandating senior assessment of Powers, Passenger, and Passage.
Incorrect: The passive second stage occurs only after full dilatation (10 cm) is achieved.
clinicalPearl: Whenever active-phase dilatation crosses the Action line, always evaluate the 3 Ps (Powers, Passenger, Passage) and fetal wellbeing before deciding between oxytocin augmentation and Caesarean section.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Crossing the Alert and Action lines indicates prolonged/abnormal labour (<1 cm/hr), prompting systematic evaluation of Powers, Passenger, and Passage.

sourceStation.title: Partogram — Alert Line, Action Line & Labour Pattern
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
05) Partogram given with labels A and B.
1) Identify A and B.
2) What type of labour is this woman having?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) A = Alert line (1 cm/hr cervical dilatation expected minimum from 4 cm); B = Action line (drawn 4 hours to the right of Alert line). (2) Labour pattern: Prolonged / Abnormal labour (slow cervical progress crossing Alert/Action lines — primary dysfunctional labour or secondary arrest depending on slope; requires assessment of 3 Ps: Powers, Passenger, Passage).

domain: 3.2 INTRAPARTUM CARE: PARTOGRAM & LABOUR ABNORMALITIES (6 STATIONS)
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida enters active labour at 4 cm cervical dilatation. Over the next 4 hours, her dilatation progresses steadily but slowly to 6 cm (0.5 cm/hour), crossing to the right of the Alert line from active-phase onset. She has 2 mild contractions per 10 minutes, zero skull moulding, clear liquor, a reassuring CTG, and an adequate pelvis. What is the diagnosis and most appropriate management?
options: Primary dysfunctional labour; perform amniotomy and start oxytocin augmentation
Secondary arrest of cervical dilatation; proceed to immediate Category 1 Caesarean section
Prolonged latent phase; discharge home with oral analgesia until 6 cm dilatation
Deep transverse arrest; perform rotational Kjelland's forceps extraction immediately
Obstructed labour with +++ moulding; administer intramuscular ergometrine
optionRationales: Correct: Slow cervical dilatation (<1 cm/hr) starting from the onset of active labour (≥4 cm) defines primary dysfunctional labour, most commonly due to hypotonic contractions; once CPD and fetal distress are excluded, ARM and oxytocin augmentation are indicated.
Incorrect: Secondary arrest refers to complete cessation of dilatation after initially normal active-phase progress, and immediate Category 1 CS is unnecessary without CPD or fetal distress.
Incorrect: She is already in the active phase (4 to 6 cm), not the latent phase.
Incorrect: Deep transverse arrest occurs in the second stage at full dilatation, not at 6 cm.
Incorrect: There is zero moulding and adequate pelvis (no obstruction), and ergometrine is strictly contraindicated before delivery of the baby.
clinicalPearl: Distinguish primary dysfunctional labour (slow slope <1 cm/hr from onset of active phase, usually inadequate powers) from secondary arrest (initial normal slope followed by complete stop, often CPD/malposition).

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Primary dysfunctional labour (<1 cm/hr from active-phase onset) without CPD or fetal distress is managed by amniotomy and titrated IV oxytocin.

sourceStation.title: Partogram — Primary Dysfunctional Labour
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
3. Photograph of a partogram showing cervical dilatation crossing the Alert line from active-phase onset.
What is the labour pattern?  [Partogram image omitted on slide in original Drive PPTX]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Primary dysfunctional labour (protracted active phase with dilatation rate below 1 cm/hr from onset of active labour, usually due to inadequate uterine contractions — manage with amniotomy/oxytocin augmentation after ruling out CPD).

domain: 3.2 INTRAPARTUM CARE: PARTOGRAM & LABOUR ABNORMALITIES (6 STATIONS)
stem: In a woman in active labour, her plotted cervical dilatation crosses to the right of the second diagonal line on the partograph grid shown. Following senior obstetric reassessment, which clinical finding mandates immediate Caesarean delivery rather than oxytocin augmentation?
options: Hypotonic uterine contractions (2 per 10 minutes) with clear amniotic liquor
Intact membranes with reassuring baseline fetal heart rate of 140 bpm
Occipito-anterior vertex position with 2/5 head palpable and zero moulding
Adequate maternal pelvic dimensions with mild caput succedaneum
Cephalopelvic disproportion with +++ irreducible skull moulding and fetal distress
optionRationales: Incorrect: Hypotonic contractions with clear liquor and no CPD are an indication for amniotomy and oxytocin augmentation.
Incorrect: Intact membranes and a normal FHR permit amniotomy and careful oxytocin augmentation if pelvic adequacy is confirmed.
Incorrect: Favourable OA position, ongoing descent (2/5), and absence of moulding rule against mechanical obstruction.
Incorrect: Mild caput alone with an adequate pelvis does not contraindicate cautious augmentation.

Correct: Crossing the Action line in the presence of cephalopelvic disproportion (+++ irreducible skull moulding) or fetal distress strictly contraindicates oxytocin and necessitates emergency Caesarean section to prevent uterine rupture and fetal asphyxia.
clinicalPearl: Never administer oxytocin in a multigravida or primigravida who shows signs of obstructed labour (+++ moulding, severe caput, haematuria, Bandl's ring) — proceed directly to Caesarean section.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Crossing the Action line mandates senior reassessment: augment with ARM/oxytocin only after excluding CPD and fetal distress; otherwise perform Caesarean section.

sourceStation.title: Partogram — Alert Line & Management Beyond Action Line
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
17. A partogram was given with lines A and B labelled.
17.1 Identify A and B.
17.2 Write the management if the cervical dilatation curve gets across line B.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (17.1) A = Alert line; B = Action line. (17.2) Management if crossing Action line: Full senior obstetric reassessment of maternal/fetal wellbeing and the 3 Ps (uterine contractions, fetal size/malposition/caput/moulding, pelvic adequacy): if no CPD/fetal distress and contractions inadequate → ARM + IV Oxytocin augmentation with repeat VE in 2–4 hours; if CPD, malpresentation, or fetal distress → Emergency Caesarean section.

domain: 3.2 INTRAPARTUM CARE: PARTOGRAM & LABOUR ABNORMALITIES (6 STATIONS)
stem: On the partograph shown, two diagonal reference lines are labelled A and B. What do lines A and B represent, and what is the standard horizontal time interval separating them?
options: A is the Action line and B is the Alert line, separated by 2 hours
A is the Latent line and B is the Active line, separated by 6 hours
A is the Alert line (1 cm/hour) and B is the Action line, placed 4 hours to the right
A is the Descent line and B is the Moulding line, separated by 3 hours
A is the Alert line (2 cm/hour) and B is the Delivery line, placed 4 hours to the right
optionRationales: Incorrect: The leftmost line (A) is the Alert line and the rightmost parallel line (B) is the Action line, separated by 4 hours rather than 2 hours.
Incorrect: Neither line represents the latent phase; both plot expected active-phase progression starting from ≥4 cm.

Correct: Line A is the Alert line sloping at 1 cm/hour (flagging slow progress or need for transfer from peripheral units), and Line B is the Action line placed 4 hours to the right (mandating definitive intervention).
Incorrect: Fetal head descent and moulding are plotted separately and do not have diagonal Alert/Action lines.
Incorrect: The minimum acceptable active-phase cervical dilatation rate on the partogram is 1 cm/hour, not 2 cm/hour.
clinicalPearl: In peripheral maternity units without operative facilities, crossing the Alert line (A) triggers early transfer to a specialist EmOC hospital before the Action line (B) is reached 4 hours later.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Alert line rises at 1 cm/hour from first detection of ≥4 cm dilatation; Action line is drawn parallel 4 hours to the right.

sourceStation.title: Partogram — Purpose of Alert & Action Lines
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
07. This is a partogram.
7.1 What is depicted by A and B?
7.2 What does line A depict?
7.3 How do you use line B in managing women in labour?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (7.1) A = Alert line; B = Action line. (7.2) Alert line (A): Represents the normal minimum rate of cervical dilatation in active labour (1 cm/hour starting at 4 cm); crossing it alerts the clinician to slow progress, prompting closer reassessment (or transfer from peripheral unit to EmOC centre). (7.3) Action line (B): Placed 4 hours to the right of Alert line; crossing it mandates definitive clinical intervention — rule out CPD/fetal distress, then augment with amniotomy/oxytocin if hypotonic, or proceed to Caesarean section if obstructed/compromised.

domain: 3.2 INTRAPARTUM CARE: PARTOGRAM & LABOUR ABNORMALITIES (6 STATIONS)
stem: At 9:00 a.m., a 39-year-old woman at 37 weeks + 5 days of gestation is assessed in active labour: fetal heart rate is 130 bpm, cervical dilatation is 5 cm, fetal head descent is 0/5 palpable per abdomen, and she has 3 contractions lasting 30 seconds each in 10 minutes. How should cervical dilatation, head descent, and contractions be charted in the 9:00 a.m. column?
options: Dilatation as O at 5 cm; head descent as X at 0/5; 3 solidly blackened contraction boxes
Dilatation as X on Alert line (5 cm); descent as O at 0/5; 3 diagonally hatched boxes
Dilatation as X at 5 cm; head descent as O at 5/5; 3 dotted contraction boxes
Dilatation as a circle at 5 cm; head descent as X at 0/5; 2 diagonally hatched contraction boxes
Dilatation as X 4 hours right of Alert line; head descent as O at 3/5; 3 dotted contraction boxes
optionRationales: Incorrect: Cervical dilatation is plotted with an 'X' and descent with an 'O' (not reversed), and 30-second contractions are shaded with diagonal lines rather than solid black (>40 s).

Correct: On the partograph, cervical dilatation is marked 'X' directly on the Alert line at 5 cm, abdominal head descent is marked 'O' at 0/5 (fully engaged), and 3 contractions lasting 20–40 seconds are charted as 3 diagonally hatched vertical squares.
Incorrect: Fully engaged head (0/5 palpable) is plotted at 0, not 5/5, and dotted shading denotes mild contractions (<20 s).
Incorrect: Using a circle for dilatation and 'X' for descent reverses standard symbols, and 3 contractions require 3 vertical boxes.
Incorrect: Initial active-phase dilatation (≥4 cm) is always plotted directly on the Alert line, not 4 hours to its right.
clinicalPearl: Partogram symbol check: X = cervix dilatation, O = head descent (5/5 floating down to 0/5 fully engaged); Contraction shading: dots (<20 s), diagonal hatching (20–40 s), solid black (>40 s).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Plot cervical dilatation with X on the Alert line, abdominal descent with O, and contractions by duration shading (dots <20 s, diagonal 20–40 s, solid >40 s).

sourceStation.title: Plotting a Partograph (9 am Findings)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
1. Plot below details in a partograph:
A 39-year-old mother with a pregnancy of 37.5 weeks (source text typo '7.5 weeks') presented with abdominal pain and dribbling.
Time: 9 a.m. | Fetal heart rate: 130 bpm | 3 contractions with 3-min intervals within 10 minutes | Descent of the fetal head was 0/5.  [Text-only plotting station]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Partograph plotting at 9:00 am column: (1) Time: Enter `09:00`; (2) FHR: Plot dot at 130 bpm; (3) Liquor: Record C (clear) or M (meconium) if dribbling observed on VE; (4) Cervix & Descent: Plot descent of head as O at 0/5 palpable (fully engaged) and cervical dilatation `X` on the Alert line at starting dilation; (5) Contractions/10 min: Shade 3 vertical boxes (use diagonal hatching for 20–40 s moderate or solid black if > 40 s strong).

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old woman in early labour undergoes the fetal surveillance tracing shown. Applying the DR C BRAVADO framework, what is the accurate interpretation and classification of this tracing?
options: Baseline 100 bpm, absent variability, and recurrent late decelerations — Pathological trace
Baseline 170 bpm, reduced variability, and variable decelerations — Suspicious CTG trace
Baseline 140 bpm, sinusoidal pattern, and absent accelerations — Pathological CTG trace
Baseline 120 bpm, early decelerations, and uterine tachysystole — Suspicious CTG trace
Baseline 140 bpm, normal variability, accelerations present, no decelerations — Normal
optionRationales: Incorrect: The fetal heart baseline sits steadily around 140 bpm with brisk oscillations and upward accelerations, not bradycardia or late decelerations.
Incorrect: Transient upward spikes above 160 bpm represent reassuring accelerations rather than a sustained baseline tachycardia of 170 bpm.
Incorrect: A sinusoidal trace shows smooth undulating waves without short-term beat-to-beat variability, whereas this trace displays crisp normal variability.
Incorrect: The uterine contraction frequency is approximately 3 in 10 minutes (normal, not tachysystole >5/10 min) and no decelerations occur.

Correct: The CTG demonstrates a normal baseline FHR of ~140 bpm (110–160), normal baseline variability of ~15–20 bpm (5–25), reassuring accelerations ≥15 bpm for ≥15 s, and zero decelerations — a Normal/Reactive CTG.
clinicalPearl: In a Normal/Reactive CTG, all four core parameters are reassuring: baseline 110–160 bpm, variability 5–25 bpm, absence of decelerations, and presence of accelerations (≥15 bpm for ≥15 s).

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Normal CTG criteria: baseline FHR 110–160 bpm, variability 5–25 bpm, no decelerations, and reassuring accelerations.

sourceStation.title: Normal Reactive Cardiotocograph (CTG)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Q.3
A.) Comment on 4 things about this CTG.
B.) What is your diagnosis about the CTG?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (A) DR C BRAVADO / 4 core features: Baseline rate = 140 bpm (normal 110–160); Baseline variability = 20 bpm (normal 5–25 bpm); Accelerations = Present; Decelerations = Absent. (B) Diagnosis: Normal / Reactive (Reassuring) CTG.

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: Three term intrauterine fetal orientations are illustrated from left to right. Which sequence correctly identifies the presentation and lie of each fetus from left to right?
options: Cephalic presentation (longitudinal lie), Breech presentation (longitudinal lie), Shoulder presentation (transverse lie)
Breech presentation (longitudinal lie), Cephalic presentation (longitudinal lie), Oblique presentation (longitudinal lie)
Face presentation (longitudinal lie), Footling breech (transverse lie), Cephalic presentation (transverse lie)
Cephalic presentation (oblique lie), Complete breech (transverse lie), Dorsal presentation (longitudinal lie)
Vertex presentation (transverse lie), Frank breech (longitudinal lie), Breech presentation (oblique lie)
optionRationales: Correct: Left shows the fetal head lowermost along the maternal vertical axis (cephalic presentation, longitudinal lie); middle shows the buttocks/podalic pole lowermost (breech presentation, longitudinal lie); right shows the fetal long axis perpendicular to the maternal spine with the shoulder over the os (shoulder presentation, transverse lie).
Incorrect: The leftmost fetus is cephalic rather than breech, and the rightmost fetus lies horizontally across the uterus (transverse lie).
Incorrect: The leftmost fetus has a well-flexed head (vertex, not face), and a breech presentation along the vertical uterine axis is longitudinal lie, not transverse.
Incorrect: Both left and middle fetuses have longitudinal lies parallel to the maternal spine, and the right fetus has a transverse lie.
Incorrect: Vertex presentation is associated with longitudinal lie, not transverse lie.
clinicalPearl: Fetal 'lie' describes the relationship of the fetal longitudinal axis to the maternal longitudinal axis (longitudinal, transverse, or oblique), whereas 'presentation' names the lowest fetal pole occupying the pelvic brim.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Longitudinal lie occurs in cephalic and breech presentations; transverse lie results in shoulder presentation, which risks cord or arm prolapse.

sourceStation.title: Fetal Presentation & Lie (Diagrams A, B, C)
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 1) State the presentation and lie for diagrams A, B, and C.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: Cephalic (vertex) presentation, Longitudinal lie; B: Breech (buttock) presentation, Longitudinal lie; C: Shoulder presentation, Transverse lie.

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: On the antenatal fetal surveillance tracing shown, four recording channels are labelled A, B, C, and D. Which option correctly identifies all four labelled channels?
options: A = Maternal heart rate; B = Oxytocin infusion boluses; C = Fetal breathing movements; D = Fetal heart rate
A = Uterine contractions; B = Cervical dilatation ticks; C = Maternal blood pressure; D = Fetal movements
A = Fetal heart rate; B = Contraction peaks; C = Baseline variability; D = Maternal pulse rate
A = Fetal heart rate; B = Maternal perception event marks; C = Fetal movements; D = Uterine contractions
A = Tocodynamometry; B = Amniotomy time marks; C = Fetal heart rate; D = Maternal perception event marks
optionRationales: Incorrect: The upper grid (60–200 bpm) records fetal heart rate via Doppler ultrasound rather than maternal heart rate, and the lower baseline records uterine activity.
Incorrect: Uterine contractions are recorded on the bottom tocodynamometer trace (D), not the upper FHR channel (A).
Incorrect: Channel B shows vertical pen ticks triggered when the mother presses the handheld event button upon feeling kicks, not contraction peaks.

Correct: A is the continuous fetal heart rate (FHR) tracing; B marks maternal perception of fetal movements (event marker); C is the automated fetal movement actogram; D is the tocodynamometer trace measuring uterine contractions.
Incorrect: Tocodynamometry corresponds to channel D at the bottom of the paper, whereas channel A is FHR.
clinicalPearl: Key indications for antenatal CTG include reduced fetal movements, PIH/pre-eclampsia, GDM, suspected IUGR/SGA, oligohydramnios, and post-term pregnancy.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: CTG traces record upper FHR, maternal perception event marks, automated actogram fetal movements, and lower tocodynamometer uterine contractions.

sourceStation.title: Cardiotocograph (CTG) Components & Indications
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5) Regarding the following investigation report:
a. Identify test.
b. Identify A, B, C, and D.
c. When to request — give 2 indications.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (a) Cardiotocograph (CTG) (note Drive slide had typo 'Non stress portogram'; correct term is Cardiotocograph / Non-Stress Test). (b) A: Fetal heart rate (FHR); B: Maternal perception event markers (button pressed by mother); C: Fetal movements (automated actogram); D: Uterine contractions (tocodynamometer). (c) Indications: Reduced fetal movements, High-risk pregnancies (PIH/pre-eclampsia, GDM, IUGR/SGA, oligohydramnios, post-dates), Intrapartum monitoring in high-risk/induced/augmented labour.

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: During intrapartum monitoring of a 31-year-old woman in active labour, the cardiotocograph reveals a baseline fetal heart rate of 135 bpm, reduced variability of 2 bpm for the past 60 minutes, and recurrent late decelerations over 30 minutes. How is this CTG classified, and what is the immediate priority action?
options: Normal CTG; continue routine intermittent auscultation every 15 minutes
Suspicious CTG; repeat cardiotocography after 2 hours of maternal ambulation
Pathological CTG; initiate intrauterine resuscitation and prepare for expedited delivery
Suspicious CTG; administer intramuscular pethidine to restore baseline variability
Normal physiological fetal sleep pattern; continue observation without intervention
optionRationales: Incorrect: Reduced variability (<5 bpm for >50 minutes) and recurrent late decelerations are both abnormal features incompatible with a Normal CTG.
Incorrect: Having two abnormal features classifies the trace as Pathological rather than Suspicious, and delaying action for 2 hours risks severe fetal acidosis.

Correct: Reduced variability (<5 bpm >50 min) combined with recurrent late decelerations constitutes a Pathological CTG, requiring immediate intrauterine resuscitation (stop oxytocin, left lateral position, IV fluid bolus, rule out cord prolapse) and urgent preparations for expedited delivery.
Incorrect: Opioid analgesia (pethidine) further depresses baseline variability and does not treat fetal hypoxia.
Incorrect: Fetal sleep cycles reduce variability typically for <40–50 minutes without recurrent late decelerations.
clinicalPearl: Intrauterine resuscitation steps for a pathological CTG: stop oxytocin infusion, place mother in left lateral position, give IV crystalloid bolus, perform VE to exclude cord prolapse/full dilatation, and prepare for expedited delivery.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Pathological CTG (e.g., variability <5 bpm >50 min or recurrent late decelerations) requires immediate intrauterine resuscitation and expedited delivery.

sourceStation.title: Cardiotocograph (CTG) Interpretation
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 2. Comment on this cardiotocograph (CTG).  [CTG image omitted on slide in original Drive PPTX]
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Systematic CTG framework (DR C BRAVADO): DR (Define Risk), C (Contractions/10 min), BRa (Baseline FHR: normal 110–160 bpm), V (Variability: normal 5–25 bpm), A (Accelerations: ≥ 15 bpm for ≥ 15 s), D (Decelerations: early, variable, or late), O (Overall impression: Normal / Suspicious / Pathological per NICE criteria).

domainClean: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: Immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes in a multiparous woman in active labour, the acute clinical finding shown in the photograph is observed at the introitus. Which predisposing obstetric factor is most strongly associated with this emergency, and what is the immediate priority action?
options: Post-term pregnancy with an engaged vertex; apply fundal pressure to expedite delivery
Footling breech malpresentation; elevate the presenting part manually and perform emergency CS
Oligohydramnios with occipito-anterior vertex; push the protruding structure back inside the uterine cavity
Grand multiparity with cephalic engagement at 0/5; commence intravenous oxytocin immediately
Placenta praevia with intact membranes; place the patient in lithotomy and await spontaneous birth
optionRationales: Incorrect: An engaged vertex fills the pelvic brim and prevents descent of the umbilical cord; fundal pressure worsens cord compression.

Correct: The photograph shows umbilical cord prolapse alongside a foot (footling breech); unengaged malpresentations (especially footling breech and transverse lie) and polyhydramnios are major risk factors, requiring manual elevation of the presenting part (or bladder filling/knee-chest/Trendelenburg positioning) and Category 1 Caesarean section.
Incorrect: Cord prolapse is associated with polyhydramnios rather than oligohydramnios, and the cord must be kept warm and moist with minimal handling rather than forcibly pushed back.
Incorrect: Oxytocin increases uterine compression against the prolapsed cord and precipitates acute fetal hypoxia.
Incorrect: Cord prolapse occurs only after membrane rupture and demands immediate emergency delivery rather than expectant management.
clinicalPearl: In cord prolapse, relieve pressure off the cord immediately by digitally elevating the presenting part vaginally (or filling the urinary bladder with 500 mL saline and placing mother in exaggerated Sims'/knee-chest/Trendelenburg position) until emergency Caesarean delivery.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Cord prolapse risk factors include footling breech, transverse lie, polyhydramnios, prematurity, and high presenting part at ARM; elevate presenting part and deliver immediately.

sourceStation.title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
sourceStation.originalPrompt:

4.2 Name three (03) predisposing risk factors.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Umbilical cord prolapse. (4.2) Predisposing risk factors: Malpresentation (breech — especially footling, transverse/oblique lie), Polyhydramnios, Preterm labour / Low birth weight, High/unengaged presenting part at amniotomy (ARM), Multiple pregnancy (2nd twin), Long umbilical cord / low-lying placenta.

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: Three fetal orientations are labelled A, B, and C in the diagram. Which option correctly matches each labelled presentation with its anatomical denominator or primary clinical management at term?
options: A = Occiput denominator; B = Sacrum denominator; C = Transverse lie requiring Caesarean birth at term
A = Denominator is the mentum; B = Denominator is the acromion; C = Safe for spontaneous vaginal delivery at term
A = Contraindication to vaginal birth; B = Denominator is the frontal bone; C = Managed routinely by vacuum extraction
A = Denominator is the sacrum; B = Denominator is the occiput; C = Presents with the suboccipitobregmatic diameter
A = Requires elective Caesarean section; B = Managed by internal podalic version at 32 weeks; C = Denominator is the bregma
optionRationales: Correct: A is cephalic vertex presentation (denominator: occiput), B is breech presentation (denominator: sacrum), and C is shoulder presentation in transverse lie (denominator: acromion), which carries high risk of hand/cord prolapse and requires Caesarean section if persistent at term.
Incorrect: The mentum is the denominator for face presentation and the acromion for shoulder presentation; term transverse lie cannot deliver vaginally.
Incorrect: Well-flexed vertex (A) is the normal presentation for vaginal delivery, and vacuum extraction is strictly contraindicated in transverse lie.
Incorrect: This reverses the denominators of vertex (occiput) and breech (sacrum), and the suboccipitobregmatic diameter belongs to well-flexed vertex.
Incorrect: Internal podalic version is reserved only for a transverse second twin at delivery, not at 32 weeks, and vertex (A) does not require routine CS.
clinicalPearl: Know the presenting denominators: Vertex = Occiput; Face = Mentum; Breech = Sacrum; Shoulder (transverse lie) = Acromion.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Denominators are occiput (vertex) and sacrum (breech); persistent transverse lie (shoulder) risks hand/cord prolapse and mandates Caesarean delivery.

stem: In the lateral diagram of the fetal skull with five numbered diameters, which option correctly matches diameters 1, 4, and 5 with their anatomical names and presenting attitudes?
options: 1: Occipitofrontal (brow); 4: Suboccipitobregmatic (vertex); 5: Submentobregmatic (deflexed OP)
1: Mentovertical (brow); 4: Submentobregmatic (face); 5: Suboccipitobregmatic (well-flexed vertex)
1: Suboccipitofrontal (deflexed vertex); 4: Occipitofrontal (vertex); 5: Mentovertical (brow)
1: Suboccipitobregmatic (well-flexed vertex); 4: Mentovertical (brow); 5: Submentobregmatic (face)
1: Submentobregmatic (face); 4: Occipitofrontal (OP vertex); 5: Suboccipitobregmatic (well-flexed vertex)
optionRationales: Incorrect: Diameter 1 connects the bregma to the suboccipital region (suboccipitobregmatic), whereas diameter 4 spans from the chin to the vertex (mentovertical).
Incorrect: Mentovertical is line 4 (chin to vertex) and suboccipitobregmatic is line 1, not vice versa.
Incorrect: Line 2 is suboccipitofrontal and line 3 is occipitofrontal; lines 1, 4, and 5 represent suboccipitobregmatic, mentovertical, and submentobregmatic.

Correct: Line 1 runs from subocciput to bregma (suboccipitobregmatic, 9.5 cm, well-flexed vertex); line 4 runs from chin/mentum to vertex (mentovertical/verticomental, 13.5 cm, brow presentation); line 5 runs from submental region to bregma (submentobregmatic, 9.5 cm, face presentation).
Incorrect: Line 5 is submentobregmatic (face) and line 1 is suboccipitobregmatic (vertex), which are reversed in this choice.
clinicalPearl: Memorise the three classic 9.5 cm vs 13.5 cm landmarks: well-flexed Vertex = Suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm), Face = Submentobregmatic (9.5 cm), Brow = Mentovertical (13.5 cm — largest diameter, cannot deliver vaginally at term).

guideCitation.keyPoint: Presenting diameters: Suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm, flexed vertex), Mentovertical (13.5 cm, brow), and Submentobregmatic (9.5 cm, face).

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: A 32-year-old uncomplicated primigravida is induced with amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin. Two hours later, her cervix is 4 cm dilated (1/5 head palpable per abdomen) with clear amniotic liquor, and the cardiotocograph shown is obtained. What is the diagnosis and mandatory immediate first action?
options: Benign early head-compression decelerations; reassure the mother and continue the oxytocin infusion
Oligohydramnios cord compression; increase the oxytocin infusion rate to achieve full dilatation
Physiological fetal sleep cycle; reposition the mother supine and repeat the tracing in 45 minutes
Impending uterine rupture; perform immediate outlet ventouse delivery at 4 cm cervical dilatation
Acute fetal distress; stop oxytocin immediately and initiate intrauterine resuscitation measures
optionRationales: Incorrect: The trace shows repeated deep abrupt decelerations down to 60 bpm, which are pathological rather than benign early decelerations.
Incorrect: Accelerating oxytocin during severe intrapartum decelerations worsens placental hypoperfusion and precipitates severe fetal acidaemia.
Incorrect: Fetal sleep does not cause repetitive severe decelerations to 60 bpm, and supine positioning worsens aortocaval compression.
Incorrect: Ventouse delivery is strictly contraindicated before full cervical dilatation (10 cm).

Correct: Deep recurrent decelerations triggered during oxytocin induction represent acute fetal distress (likely uterine hyperstimulation/tachysystole); the immediate first step is to stop oxytocin, reposition left lateral, give IV fluids (± acute tocolytic e.g. SC terbutaline 0.25 mg), perform VE to exclude cord prolapse, and prepare for Category 1 Caesarean section if unresolved.
clinicalPearl: Stopping the oxytocin infusion is always the single fastest first intervention for oxytocin-induced fetal distress, rapidly restoring intervillous blood flow within minutes.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Pathological CTG during oxytocin induction mandates immediate cessation of oxytocin, left lateral positioning, IV fluid bolus, VE, and expedited delivery if persistent.

sourceStation.title: Oxytocin Hyperstimulation & Fetal Distress (Pathological CTG)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04. A 32-year-old uncomplicated primigravida is admitted to the ward. She is induced with artificial rupture of membranes and oxytocin. Amniotic fluid is clear. On examination: 1/5 fetal head palpable in abdomen; cervix dilated up to 4 cm and fully effaced. A CTG was performed after 2 hours.
1. What is the diagnosis?
2. Outline the immediate management plan in three steps.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Diagnosis: Acute fetal distress / Pathological CTG secondary to oxytocin-induced uterine hyperstimulation (tachysystole). (2) 3-Step Immediate Management: (a) Stop oxytocin infusion immediately; (b) Intrauterine resuscitation — turn mother to left lateral position, give IV fluid bolus (crystalloid) ± acute tocolysis (e.g., SC Terbutaline 0.25 mg) if hypertonus persists, and check VE for cord prolapse / rapid full dilatation; (c) Prepare for urgent Category 1 Emergency Caesarean section if CTG does not rapidly normalise (or assisted vaginal delivery only if fully dilated & head engaged).

domainClean: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS

domain: 3.3 FETAL SURVEILLANCE (CTG), FETAL LIE, PRESENTATION & PELVIS (9 STATIONS)
stem: Based on the intrauterine diagram showing the relationship of the fetal body and head to the maternal pelvis, what is the fetal position, and which landmarks are palpated on vaginal examination in labour to confirm it?
options: Left Occipito-Anterior (LOA); coronal suture and nasal bridge
Right Occipito-Anterior (ROA/ROL); sagittal suture and fontanelles
Direct Occipito-Posterior (OP); sacral promontory and fetal mentum
Left Sacro-Anterior (LSA); fetal ischial tuberosities and anus
Right Mento-Posterior (RMP); orbital ridges and frontal suture
optionRationales: Incorrect: Viewed in anatomical orientation, the smooth convex fetal back lies on the maternal right side (viewer's left), corresponding to a right-sided occiput position rather than LOA.

Correct: The flexed cephalic fetus has its smooth back on the maternal right (ROA/ROL), and intrapartum vaginal examination confirms occiput position by tracing the sagittal suture to the triangular posterior fontanelle (3 sutures) and diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle (4 sutures).
Incorrect: In direct OP, the fetal spine lies posteriorly and the chin/face is not the presenting landmark.
Incorrect: The fetus is cephalic (head lowermost), not breech (sacrum denominator).
Incorrect: The fetal neck is flexed (vertex presentation) rather than hyperextended (face presentation).
clinicalPearl: Three modalities confirm fetal position: (1) Leopold's abdominal palpation (smooth back vs small limbs), (2) Intrapartum VE (sagittal suture + triangular posterior vs diamond anterior fontanelle), and (3) Ultrasound scan.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Fetal position is determined by abdominal palpation, vaginal palpation of sagittal suture and fontanelles, or ultrasound; LOA/ROA are normal cephalic positions.

sourceStation.title: Fetal Position Assessment & Pelvic Diagram
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4. Relationship of the fetal head to the maternal pelvis.
4.1 Write 3 examination methods used to assess the position of the fetus.
4.2 What is the position of the fetus shown in the diagram?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (4.1) Examination methods: (a) Abdominal palpation (Leopold's manoeuvres / lateral grip) to locate fetal spine & limbs; (b) Vaginal examination (intrapartum) palpating sagittal suture and anterior/posterior fontanelles; (c) Ultrasound scan (transabdominal confirmation of spine/occiput). (4.2) Position shown: Right Occipito-Anterior / Right Occipito-Lateral (ROA / ROL) (vertex presentation, longitudinal lie, fetal back on maternal right).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Four instruments used in obstetrics and gynaecology are labelled A to D in the photograph. Which option correctly identifies the instrument specifically designed to grasp the cut edges of the lower uterine segment for atraumatic haemostasis during Caesarean section?
options: Instrument A (Cusco's bivalve speculum) — retracts the uterine incision edges during Caesarean section
Instrument B (Haywood Smith's ovum forceps) — evacuates retained products of conception in miscarriage
Instrument B (Green-Armytage forceps) — clamps cut uterine edges for haemostasis at Caesarean
Instrument C (Ayre's wooden spatula) — dilates the internal cervical os before uterine curettage
Instrument D (Vulsellum forceps) — steadies the anterior lip of the non-pregnant cervix during D&C
optionRationales: Incorrect: Instrument A is Cusco's self-retaining vaginal speculum used to inspect the cervix and perform Pap smears, not for Caesarean uterine edges.
Incorrect: Ovum forceps have spoon-shaped fenestrated ends without a ratchet lock, whereas B has flat triangular serrated jaws with a ratchet.

Correct: Instrument B is Green-Armytage uterine haemostatic forceps, distinguished by its broad, triangular, transversely serrated atraumatic tips used to clamp bleeding edges of the lower uterine segment during LSCS.
Incorrect: Instrument C is Ayre's wooden spatula used to scrape ectocervical transformation-zone cells for Pap cytology, not a dilator.
Incorrect: Instrument D is Spencer Wells artery forceps used to clamp bleeding vessels, hold membranes for amniotomy, or clamp the umbilical cord, whereas Vulsellum has curved toothed tips.
clinicalPearl: Green-Armytage forceps have broad triangular serrated jaws that distribute pressure evenly, controlling venous sinus bleeding from cut LSCS uterine edges without tearing fragile myometrium.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Green-Armytage forceps (triangular serrated tips) hold the cut edge of the lower uterine segment atraumatically for haemostasis during Caesarean section.

sourceStation.title: Ob/Gyn Instruments (Cusco's, Green-Armytage, Ayre's, Artery Forceps)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
Q.2
Four Ob/Gyn instruments (A, B, C, D) are shown.
Identify the instruments and give 1 use for each.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: Cusco's self-retaining bivalve vaginal speculum — visualise cervix/vaginal walls (Pap smear, IUCD insertion); B: Green-Armytage uterine/haemostatic forceps — hold cut uterine edges & achieve haemostasis during Caesarean section; C: Ayre's wooden spatula — collect ectocervical cell scrapings for Pap smear; D: Artery forceps (Spencer Wells) — clamp bleeding vessels / hold membranes for ARM or umbilical cord clamping.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Among the four gynaecological instruments numbered 1 to 4 in the photograph, what are the identity and primary clinical purpose of instrument 4?
options: Hegar's cervical dilator — performs gradual mechanical cervical dilatation before curettage
Sims' uterine sound — measures uterocervical cavity depth and direction prior to IUCD insertion
Blake's uterine curette — scrapes the endometrial cavity to obtain a histological tissue biopsy
Karman's suction cannula — performs manual vacuum aspiration of first-trimester products of conception
Veress needle — creates carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum at the umbilicus during laparoscopy
optionRationales: Correct: Instrument 4 is a curved cylindrical Hegar's cervical dilator (graduated in millimetres), inserted sequentially from smaller to larger sizes to dilate the cervical os prior to D&C, hysteroscopy, or ERPC.
Incorrect: The uterine sound is shown in panel 3 (slender graduated rod with flat ribbed handle), not panel 4.
Incorrect: Blake's uterine curette has fenestrated spoon-shaped loops at its ends rather than a smooth solid cylindrical shaft.
Incorrect: Karman's cannula is a flexible plastic suction catheter with distal side apertures.
Incorrect: A Veress needle is a sharp spring-loaded insufflation needle with a hub stopcock.
clinicalPearl: When dilating the cervix with Hegar's dilators, hold the instrument like a pen and apply gentle axial pressure in the direction of the uterus (determined beforehand by bimanual exam and uterine sounding) to prevent false passage or perforation.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Hegar's dilators are graduated curved rods (3–26 mm) used for serial mechanical cervical dilatation prior to D&C, hysteroscopy, or evacuation.

sourceStation.title: Five Classic Ob/Gyn Instruments
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01. Five gynaecological/obstetric instruments are shown (Sims' speculum, Cusco's bivalve speculum, Vulsellum, Uterine sound, Cervical/Hegar dilator).
Identify the instruments.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Sims' speculum — retract posterior vaginal wall to inspect anterior wall (cystocele), Pap smear, IUCD, HSG; (2) Cusco's bivalve speculum — self-retaining cervix visualisation; (3) Vulsellum forceps — grasp anterior lip of cervix (IUCD insertion, cervical biopsy, D&C); (4) Uterine sound — measure uterocervical cavity length/direction; (5) Hegar cervical dilator — gradual mechanical cervical dilatation (D&C, hysteroscopy, cervical stenosis).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: In the anatomical diagram of the external female genitalia with landmarks labelled A to E, which sequence correctly identifies all five labelled structures?
options: A = Labia minora; B = Labia majora; C = Mons pubis; D = Vaginal introitus; E = Perineal body
A = Labia majora; B = Labia minora; C = Clitoris; D = External urethral opening; E = Posterior fourchette
A = Labia majora; B = Vestibular bulb; C = Urethral meatus; D = Clitoris; E = Bartholin's duct
A = Inguinal fold; B = Labia minora; C = Clitoral hood; D = Hymenal ring; E = Anal verge
A = Labia majora; B = Skene's gland; C = Clitoris; D = Vaginal rugae; E = Posterior fourchette
optionRationales: Incorrect: Label A indicates the outer cutaneous fold (labia majora) and B indicates the inner mucosal fold (labia minora).

Correct: A is the labia majora, B is the labia minora, C is the anterior midline glans clitoris, D is the external urethral meatus, and E is the posterior fourchette where the labia minora unite posteriorly.
Incorrect: Labels C (clitoris) and D (urethral meatus) are inverted, and E marks the midline posterior fourchette rather than the lateral Bartholin's duct.
Incorrect: Label D points to the anterior urethral opening above the vaginal orifice, not the hymenal ring, and E is above the perineal body and anus.
Incorrect: Label B points directly to the folded labia minora and D points to the urethral meatus rather than vaginal rugae.
clinicalPearl: Know the anterior-to-posterior midline landmarks of the vestibule: Clitoris → External urethral meatus (with Skene's ducts) → Vaginal introitus (with Bartholin's ducts at 4 & 8 o'clock) → Posterior fourchette.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Vulval anatomical sequence from outer to inner and anterior to posterior: Labia majora, Labia minora, Clitoris, External urethral opening, and Posterior fourchette.

sourceStation.title: External Female Genitalia (Vulval Anatomy A–E)

02. This is a photograph/diagram of the vulva with labelled parts A–E.
Identify the labelled parts.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A = Labia majora (outer cutaneous fold); B = Labia minora (inner mucosal fold); C = Clitoris (anterior midline erectile structure); D = Urethral opening (external urethral meatus); E = Posterior fourchette / Vestibular (navicular) fossa.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Two vaginal specula are displayed side by side in the photograph. Which option accurately contrasts their identification and primary clinical applications?
options: The left instrument is self-retaining and leaves both hands free for cervical cytology sampling
The right instrument is preferred in Sims' left lateral position to inspect a cystocele or fistula
The left instrument covers both the anterior and posterior vaginal walls simultaneously
Left (Sims' speculum) assesses rectocele; right (Cusco's speculum) is self-retaining to view cervix
The right instrument (Sims' speculum) requires an assistant to hold it in place during a Pap smear
optionRationales: Incorrect: The left instrument is Sims' duck-bill speculum, which is NOT self-retaining and must be held manually; Cusco's (right) is self-retaining.
Incorrect: Inspection of anterior wall prolapse (cystocele) or vesicovaginal fistula in Sims' left lateral position requires Sims' speculum (left), not Cusco's.
Incorrect: Cusco's bivalve speculum (right) obscures the anterior and posterior vaginal walls with its blades, making it unsuitable for assessing prolapse.

Correct: Left is Sims' double-bladed speculum (retracting one vaginal wall in Sims' position to visualise rectocele, cystocele, or VVF), while right is Cusco's self-retaining bivalve speculum (exposing the cervix for Pap smear or IUCD insertion).
Incorrect: The right instrument is Cusco's speculum (not Sims'), and its screw mechanism renders it self-retaining.
clinicalPearl: Exam classic: use Cusco's speculum to inspect the cervix (Pap smear, HVS, IUCD), but switch to Sims' speculum in Sims' left lateral position to inspect vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele/rectocele) or VVF.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Sims' speculum retracts a single vaginal wall to assess prolapse (cystocele/rectocele) or VVF; Cusco's self-retaining bivalve speculum visualises the cervix.

sourceStation.title: Sims' vs Cusco's Speculum Clinical Distinction
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
01. Identify the two instruments shown.
Which is used for rectocele visualisation and which is to visualise the cervix?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Sims' speculum → used in Sims' position to retract the anterior vaginal wall and visualise a rectocele (or retract posterior wall for cystocele); Cusco's bivalve speculum → self-retaining speculum to visualise the cervix (and perform Pap smear).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Two outpatient gynaecological clinic items are displayed side by side. Which pairing accurately describes the primary clinical purpose of the left and right instruments respectively?
options: Left: performs outpatient endometrial aspiration; Right: dilates the endocervical canal
Left: samples the ectocervical transformation zone; Right: supports uterovaginal prolapse
Left: measures uterocervical cavity length; Right: occludes the fallopian tubes permanently
Left: clamps the anterior cervical lip; Right: maintains vaginal patency after radiotherapy
Left: scrapes vulval skin lesions for fungal hyphae; Right: delivers intravaginal prostaglandins
optionRationales: Incorrect: Outpatient endometrial aspiration uses a Pipelle sampler rather than an Ayre's wooden spatula, and cervical dilatation uses Hegar dilators.
Correct: The left item is an Ayre's wooden spatula for Pap smear cytology at the transformation zone, and the right item is a vaginal ring pessary for conservative support of pelvic organ prolapse.
Incorrect: Measuring uterocervical cavity length requires a graduated uterine sound, and a vaginal ring pessary does not provide tubal contraception.
Incorrect: Grasping the anterior cervical lip requires a vulsellum or sponge-holding forceps rather than a wooden spatula.
Incorrect: An Ayre's spatula is specifically contoured with a bifid end for cervical cytology rather than vulval skin scrapings, and a ring pessary is mechanical rather than prostaglandin-eluting.
clinicalPearl: In a conventional Pap smear, the longer prong of the Ayre's spatula rotates 360 degrees at the external os to sample the transformation zone, whereas a ring pessary supports prolapsed pelvic organs when surgery is declined or contraindicated.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Ayre's spatula samples the ectocervical transformation zone for CIN screening; a vaginal ring pessary provides conservative mechanical support for uterovaginal prolapse.

sourceStation.title: Ayre's Wooden Spatula & Vaginal Ring Pessary
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 02. Identify and give one use of each instrument shown (Ayre's wooden spatula, vaginal ring pessary).
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Ayre's wooden spatula — collect cervical cytology smear (Pap smear) to screen for CIN/cervical carcinoma. Vaginal ring pessary — conservative non-surgical support for pelvic organ prolapse (uterovaginal prolapse, cystocele, rectocele) or stress urinary incontinence.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 39 weeks' gestation has been actively pushing for 90 minutes in the second stage of labour when persistent late decelerations develop on CTG. Examination confirms full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, and an occipito-anterior vertex at station +2 with 0/5 head palpable abdominally. Which identification and indication best describe the illustrated instrument?
options: Wrigley's outlet forceps designed solely for delivering the fetal head during Caesarean section
Kielland's rotational forceps with a sliding lock for correcting deep transverse arrest
Green-Armytage haemostatic forceps used to clamp bleeding lower-segment uterine edges
Simpson's obstetric forceps indicated for prolonged second stage or second-stage fetal distress
Haywood-Smith ovum forceps used to evacuate retained products of conception in miscarriage
optionRationales: Incorrect: Wrigley's forceps have very short shanks and handles for outlet deliveries or Caesarean sections, whereas this instrument has long shanks and dark grooved handles with finger guards.
Incorrect: Kielland's forceps have straight shanks, a minimal pelvic curve, and a sliding lock, unlike this long-shanked instrument with a pronounced pelvic curve and English lock.
Incorrect: Green-Armytage forceps are atraumatic triangular-tipped surgical clamps used at Caesarean section, not fenestrated cephalic traction blades.

Correct: Simpson's obstetric forceps feature long shanks, cephalic and pelvic curves, and fenestrated blades suited for traction in prolonged second stage, fetal distress, maternal exhaustion, or the after-coming head of a breech.
Incorrect: Ovum forceps have spoon-shaped fenestrated jaws with no ratchet lock and are used in miscarriage evacuation rather than live term vaginal delivery.
clinicalPearl: Simpson's forceps have elongated blades that accommodate a moulded fetal skull and are classic for prolonged second stage, second-stage fetal distress, and maternal contraindications to bearing down.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Obstetric traction forceps feature cephalic and pelvic curves with an English lock and are indicated for second-stage delay, fetal distress, or maternal exhaustion.

sourceStation.title: Simpson Obstetric Forceps
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
2.
1. Identify this instrument.
2. Give 2 clinical uses (indications) of it.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Simpson's obstetric forceps. (2) Indications: Prolonged second stage of labour, Maternal exhaustion / medical contraindications to Valsalva (cardiac disease, severe hypertension, intracranial aneurysm), Fetal distress / non-reassuring CTG in 2nd stage, After-coming head in breech delivery (and good for moulded elongated fetal head).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 30-year-old woman in the second stage of labour develops severe maternal exhaustion with a prolonged second stage, and the obstetrician prepares to apply the illustrated outlet instrument. Which complete set of clinical prerequisites must be confirmed before application?
options: Full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged vertex head with known position, and empty bladder
Cervical dilatation of at least 8 cm, intact membranes, vertex at station 0, and regional analgesia
Full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, 2/5 head palpable abdominally, and mento-posterior attitude
Cervical dilatation of 9 cm, ruptured membranes, brow presentation at +1 station, and senior operator
Full cervical dilatation, intact membranes, high floating vertex, and prophylactic oxytocin infusion
optionRationales: Correct: Safe instrumental delivery (FORCEPS mnemonic) requires full 10 cm dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged vertex (0/5 palpable abdominally) with known exact position, empty bladder, adequate analgesia, and an experienced operator.
Incorrect: Applying obstetric forceps before full 10 cm cervical dilatation risks severe cervical laceration and uterine rupture, and membranes must be ruptured.
Incorrect: Finding 2/5 of the head palpable per abdomen indicates an unengaged head with possible cephalopelvic disproportion, and mento-posterior face presentation requires Caesarean section.
Incorrect: Incomplete dilatation (9 cm) and brow presentation (mentovertical diameter 13.5 cm) are absolute contraindications to vaginal forceps delivery.
Incorrect: Intact membranes and an unengaged high head preclude forceps application; amniotomy and reassessment for cephalopelvic disproportion are required first.
clinicalPearl: Memorise the FORCEPS prerequisites: Full dilatation, Occiput position known, Ruptured membranes, Cephalopelvic disproportion excluded (0/5 palpable, station ≥ +2), Empty bladder/analgesia, Paediatrician present, and Skilled operator.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Forceps delivery requires 10 cm dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged cephalic vertex (0/5 abdominally) with known position, empty bladder, and adequate analgesia.

sourceStation.title: Wrigley's / Simpson Outlet Obstetric Forceps & Prerequisites
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
04)
1) Identify the instrument.
2) Write four (4) prerequisites needed to be fulfilled to use this instrument.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (1) Obstetric forceps (Wrigley's outlet forceps / Simpson forceps). (2) Prerequisites ('FORCEPS' / standard 6): (a) Full cervical dilatation (10 cm) & ruptured membranes; (b) Head engaged (0/5 palpable per abdomen) & station ≥ +2 / outlet; (c) Exact fetal head position & vertex presentation known (no CPD); (d) Empty bladder & adequate analgesia; (e) Senior experienced operator + maternal consent + theatre backup.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with a dragging pelvic sensation and urinary leakage on coughing. To examine her anterior vaginal wall specifically for a cystocele or vesicovaginal fistula with the patient in Sims' left lateral position, which displayed instrument should be selected and why?
options: Instrument A, because its dual hinged blades retract the anterior wall upward for cystocele viewing
Instrument A, because it requires no assistant and exposes both vaginal walls simultaneously
Instrument B, because its screw lock renders it self-retaining during solo outpatient Pap smears
Instrument A, because its concave handle collects leaked urine for biochemical confirmation
Instrument B, because retracting the posterior wall leaves the anterior vaginal wall unobstructed
optionRationales: Incorrect: Instrument A is Cusco's bivalve speculum, whose upper and lower blades cover and compress both the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, obscuring prolapse.
Incorrect: While Cusco's speculum (A) is self-retaining, its blades cover the anterior and posterior vaginal walls rather than exposing them for prolapse assessment.
Incorrect: Instrument B (Sims' speculum) has no screw lock and is non-self-retaining, requiring an assistant to hold it in place.
Incorrect: Collecting drained blood or urine in a concave handle is a feature of Sims' speculum (B), not Cusco's speculum (A).

Correct: Instrument B is Sims' double-bladed duck-bill speculum; retracting only the posterior vaginal wall in the left lateral position provides an unobstructed view of the anterior vaginal wall for cystocele or fistula assessment.
clinicalPearl: Cusco's bivalve speculum (A) is self-retaining for Pap smears and IUCD insertion, whereas Sims' speculum (B) exposes the anterior vaginal wall to evaluate cystocele and vesicovaginal fistula.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Cusco's speculum covers vaginal walls and suits cervical visualisation; Sims' non-self-retaining speculum retracts the posterior wall to inspect anterior wall prolapse and fistulae.

sourceStation.title: Cusco's & Sims' Speculums (or Ayre's / Ring Pessary)
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
4) Instruments A and B are shown.
• Identify the instruments.
• Write 1 use for each one.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: Cusco's bivalve self-retaining vaginal speculum — visualise cervix/vaginal vault for Pap smear, high vaginal swab, or IUCD insertion. B: Sims' double-bladed vaginal speculum — inspect anterior/posterior vaginal walls for prolapse (cystocele/rectocele) and perform gynaecological procedures (with assistant).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 33-year-old woman at 38 weeks' gestation is scheduled for an elective lower-segment Caesarean section because of two previous Caesarean deliveries. Regional anaesthesia is planned using the fine-bore needle shown. Which pre-operative finding constitutes an absolute contraindication to this procedure?
options: Diet-controlled gestational diabetes mellitus with a fasting glucose of 86 mg/dL
Mild physiological anaemia of pregnancy with haemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL
Severe thrombocytopenia accompanied by disseminated intravascular coagulation
Previous Pfannenstiel transverse suprapubic surgical scar from prior deliveries
Well-controlled mild intermittent bronchial asthma using inhaled salbutamol
optionRationales: Incorrect: Well-controlled gestational diabetes is not a contraindication to spinal anaesthesia; regional blockade is preferred over general anaesthesia.
Incorrect: A haemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL in the third trimester meets the normal BCSH/SLCOG pregnancy threshold (≥10.5 g/dL) and does not preclude neuraxial anaesthesia.

Correct: Coagulopathy, severe thrombocytopenia, raised intracranial pressure, local puncture-site sepsis, and uncorrected hypovolaemia are key contraindications to obstetric spinal anaesthesia due to spinal epidural haematoma risk.
Incorrect: Previous Caesarean scars are one of the most common indications for elective Caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia.
Incorrect: Regional spinal anaesthesia is actually advantageous in bronchial asthma because it avoids airway instrumentation and bronchospasm associated with endotracheal intubation.
clinicalPearl: Always check platelet count, coagulation status, blood pressure/volume status, neurological signs (raised ICP), and lumbar skin integrity before administering spinal anaesthesia in obstetrics.

guideCitation.guideTitle: GDM & Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy (PIH) Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Spinal anaesthesia is contraindicated when raised intracranial pressure or coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia is present (as in severe pre-eclampsia/eclampsia).

sourceStation.title: Obstetric Spinal Needle — Indications & Contraindications
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
5)
• Mention a clinical situation in which this needle is used in obstetrics.
• What are the contraindications for its use?
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Clinical use: Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia for Caesarean section (or instrumental delivery/cervical cerclage/manual removal of placenta). Contraindications: Patient refusal, Coagulopathy / thrombocytopenia / therapeutic anticoagulation, Raised intracranial pressure (space-occupying lesion), Local skin infection/sepsis at lumbar puncture site, Uncorrected severe hypovolaemia / shock, Fixed cardiac output states (severe aortic/mitral stenosis).

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Four clinical examination and operative positions (A–D) are illustrated. A 54-year-old woman requires assessment for an anterior vaginal wall prolapse using a Sims' speculum, while a 28-year-old primigravida requires repair of a mediolateral episiotomy after childbirth. Which positions are most appropriate for these two procedures respectively?
options: Position B for anterior wall prolapse assessment; Position A for episiotomy repair
Position A for anterior wall prolapse assessment; Position C for episiotomy repair
Position C for anterior wall prolapse assessment; Position D for episiotomy repair
Position D for anterior wall prolapse assessment; Position B for episiotomy repair
Position A for anterior wall prolapse assessment; Position B for episiotomy repair
optionRationales: Incorrect: Position B is the dorsal recumbent position (used for routine bimanual or Cusco's speculum examination), and Position A (Sims' left lateral) is not standard for episiotomy repair.

Correct: Position A (Sims' left lateral) is optimal for inspecting anterior vaginal wall prolapse or vesicovaginal fistula with a Sims' speculum, and Position C (lithotomy) provides optimal access for delivery and perineal suturing.
Incorrect: Lithotomy (C) obscures gravity-dependent anterior prolapse positioning compared with Sims', while D is steep Trendelenburg extended lithotomy used for operative laparoscopy/hysteroscopy.
Incorrect: Position D is steep Trendelenburg lithotomy for laparoscopic pelvic surgery, and dorsal recumbent (B) lacks stirrup perineal exposure for episiotomy repair.
Incorrect: Episiotomy suturing requires lithotomy positioning (C) rather than dorsal recumbent (B) for adequate illumination and apex visualisation.
clinicalPearl: Match each position to its exam goal: Sims' (A) for cystocele/VVF, Dorsal recumbent (B) for routine bimanual/Pap smear, Lithotomy (C) for vaginal delivery and perineal repair, and Trendelenburg lithotomy (D) for pelvic laparoscopy.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Sims' left lateral position evaluates anterior vaginal wall prolapse/VVF; lithotomy position supports instrumental delivery, perineal repair, and D&C.

sourceStation.title: Four Gynaecological Examination Positions
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
19.
19.A — Name the following positions (A, B, C, D).
19.B — Name one gynaecological/obstetric intervention done in each respective position.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: Sims' (left lateral) position → examine vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele/rectocele) or vesicovaginal fistula; B: Dorsal recumbent position → bimanual pelvic examination / routine speculum exam; C: Lithotomy position → childbirth / instrumental delivery / perineal suturing; D: Extended lithotomy (Trendelenburg/steep lithotomy) → IUCD insertion / operative hysteroscopy / D&C.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with two episodes of painless vaginal bleeding 6 years after menopause, and transvaginal ultrasound reveals an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. Which illustrated instrument enables outpatient tissue diagnosis without general anaesthesia or cervical dilatation?
options: The bifurcated wooden blades at the bottom left used for ectocervical scraping
The curved fenestrated metal blades on the right fitted with an axis-traction handle
Both the bottom-left wooden instrument and the right-hand metal forceps combined
The right-hand metal instrument used to clamp the uterine artery pedicles
The flexible narrow cannula at the top left used for endometrial aspiration biopsy
optionRationales: Incorrect: The bottom-left items are Ayre's wooden spatulas, which sample surface squamous cells at the cervical transformation zone for Pap smears rather than endometrial tissue.
Incorrect: The right-hand item is obstetric traction forceps for assisted vaginal birth, not an endometrial biopsy tool.
Incorrect: Neither an Ayre's spatula nor obstetric forceps enters the endometrial cavity for histological sampling.
Incorrect: The right-hand device is obstetric forceps rather than a surgical hysterectomy clamp.
Correct: The top-left device is a Pipelle endometrial sampler, a thin flexible plastic suction curette that obtains outpatient endometrial histology for abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding.
clinicalPearl: A Pipelle endometrial biopsy is the first-line outpatient histological test for postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness > 4–5 mm, avoiding general anaesthesia.

guideCitation.keyPoint: Outpatient endometrial biopsy curettes/samplers obtain endometrial histology in abnormal or postmenopausal uterine bleeding without formal theatre dilatation and curettage.

sourceStation.title: Pipelle, Simpson Forceps, Ayre's Spatula & Green-Armytage
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 1. Identify the following instruments and give one use for each.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: Pipelle endometrial sampler → outpatient endometrial aspiration biopsy for postmenopausal/abnormal uterine bleeding; Simpson forceps → assisted vaginal delivery; Ayre's spatula → Pap smear cervical cytology scraping; Green-Armytage forceps → haemostatic clamping of uterine incision edges at Caesarean section.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Four obstetric and gynaecological devices (A–D) are shown. During active labour in a high-risk pregnancy with meconium-stained liquor, continuous electronic monitoring of fetal heart rate and uterine contractions is required, whereas in a low-risk pregnancy at 36 weeks intermittent bedside auscultation is performed. Which devices serve these two functions respectively?
options: Device B for continuous electronic monitoring; Device D for intermittent auscultation
Device A for continuous electronic monitoring; Device C for intermittent auscultation
Device D for continuous electronic monitoring; Device B for intermittent auscultation
Device C for continuous electronic monitoring; Device A for intermittent auscultation
Device B for continuous electronic monitoring; Device A for intermittent auscultation
optionRationales: Correct: Device B is a cardiotocograph (CTG) machine for continuous FHR and tocodynamometry recording, and Device D is a Pinard's fetal stethoscope (fetoscope) for direct intermittent abdominal auscultation.
Incorrect: Device A is a Kiwi OmniCup vacuum extractor for second-stage assisted birth, and Device C is Cusco's bivalve speculum for cervical inspection.
Incorrect: The roles are reversed; a Pinard fetoscope (D) performs intermittent auscultation rather than continuous graphic recording.
Incorrect: Cusco's speculum (C) and the Kiwi ventouse (A) have no role in fetal heart rate monitoring.
Incorrect: Device A is a vacuum extractor cup for operative vaginal delivery, not a fetal auscultation device.
clinicalPearl: Use a Pinard fetoscope over the fetal anterior shoulder for intermittent auscultation in low-risk labour, and continuous CTG monitoring when high-risk factors such as meconium liquor or oxytocin are present.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Cardiotocography continuously monitors FHR and uterine contractions (DR C BRAVADO); the Pinard fetoscope provides intermittent FHR auscultation from 24–28 weeks onward.

sourceStation.title: Kiwi Ventouse, CTG Machine, Cusco's Speculum & Pinard Fetoscope
sourceStation.originalPrompt: 1. Identify these instruments (A, B, C, D) and write one use for each.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: A: Kiwi OmniCup vacuum extractor (ventouse) — assisted vaginal delivery in 2nd stage (safe ≥ 34–36 weeks); B: Cardiotocograph (CTG) machine — continuous electronic monitoring of FHR and uterine contractions; C: Cusco's self-retaining bivalve speculum — inspect cervix/take Pap smear; D: Pinard's fetal stethoscope (fetoscope) — intermittent auscultation of fetal heart sounds per abdomen.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: Instruments A and B are both used for operative vaginal delivery. A 31-year-old woman at 32+3 weeks' gestation develops persistent fetal bradycardia in the second stage of labour with full cervical dilatation, ruptured membranes, and an occipito-anterior vertex at station +2. Which clinical decision regarding these two instruments is most accurate?
options: Select instrument B because gentle vacuum suction avoids facial nerve injury in preterm infants
Select either instrument A or B interchangeably since both are safe after 30 weeks' gestation
Select instrument A because vacuum suction below 34 weeks risks neonatal intracranial haemorrhage
Select instrument B because it can be safely applied even before full cervical dilatation at 32 weeks
Avoid both instruments and deliver by immediate breech extraction under spinal anaesthesia
optionRationales: Incorrect: Vacuum extraction (B) carries an unacceptably high risk of subgaleal and intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm skulls below 34 weeks' gestation.
Incorrect: Ventouse is strictly contraindicated below 34 weeks' gestation (and ideally avoided below 36 weeks) because of preterm cranial fragility.

Correct: Obstetric forceps (A) protect the premature fetal cranium during traction, whereas the Kiwi OmniCup ventouse (B) is contraindicated under 34 weeks' gestation due to subgaleal and intracranial haemorrhage risk.
Incorrect: Vacuum extraction before full dilatation in a preterm fetus increases cranial trauma and cervical injury and remains contraindicated below 34 weeks.
Incorrect: This fetus is in a cephalic vertex presentation, making breech extraction inapplicable.
clinicalPearl: Remember the three classic contraindications to ventouse (vacuum) delivery: gestation < 34 weeks, face or brow presentation, and fetal bleeding disorders.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Vacuum extraction is contraindicated at gestations < 34 weeks (risk of subgaleal/intraventricular haemorrhage), in face/brow presentations, and in fetal bleeding disorders.

sourceStation.title: Simpson Forceps & Kiwi Ventouse — Prerequisites
sourceStation.originalPrompt:
20. Instruments A and B are shown.
20.1 Identify A and B.
20.2 List four (04) prerequisites for the use of these instruments.
sourceStation.verifiedAnswer: (20.1) A = Simpson's obstetric forceps; B = Kiwi OmniCup vacuum extractor (ventouse). (20.2) Prerequisites: (1) Full cervical dilatation (10 cm) & ruptured membranes; (2) Cephalic vertex presentation, head engaged (0/5 palpable per abdomen) & exact position confirmed; (3) No cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD); (4) Empty maternal bladder, adequate analgesia, valid consent, and senior operator.

domain: 3.4 OBSTETRIC & GYNAECOLOGICAL INSTRUMENTS, POSITIONS & PROCEDURES (17 STATIONS)
stem: A 28-year-old primigravida undergoes an emergency Caesarean section under subarachnoid block performed with the illustrated cutting-bevel needles. Twelve hours postoperatively, she develops a severe fronto-occipital headache that worsens rapidly on sitting up and improves when lying supine. What is the diagnosis and pathophysiology?
options: Total spinal anaesthesia caused by cephalad spread of bupivacaine into the cervical cord
Acute epidural abscess resulting from haematogenous bacterial seeding of the subarachnoid space
Severe pre-eclamptic cerebral oedema precipitated by postoperative intravenous crystalloid loading
Post-dural puncture headache caused by persistent CSF leakage through the dural defect
Spinal epidural haematoma compressing the cauda equina following needle withdrawal
optionRationales: Incorrect: Total spinal anaesthesia presents immediately during surgery with profound hypotension, apnoea, and loss of consciousness rather than a postural headache 12 hours later.
Incorrect: An epidural abscess develops over days to weeks with fever, back pain, and progressive neurological deficits rather than an immediate postural headache.
Incorrect: Pre-eclamptic headache is typically non-postural and accompanied by severe hypertension, hyperreflexia, or visual disturbances.
Correct: Cutting-bevel (Quincke) spinal needles cut dural fibres rather than separating them, predisposing to CSF leakage, intracranial hypotension, and postural post-dural puncture headache (PDPH).
Incorrect: An epidural haematoma causes severe back pain, motor weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction rather than an isolated orthostatic headache.
clinicalPearl: Post-dural puncture headache is classically postural (worse upright, relieved supine) and occurs more frequently with larger-gauge cutting Quincke-bevel needles than pencil-point (Whitacre/Sprotte) needles.

guideCitation.guideTitle: Comprehensive Gynaecology & Obstetrics OSCE Study Guide
guideCitation.keyPoint: Key complications of Quincke-bevel spinal needles include maternal hypotension, post-dural puncture headache (PDPH), and high or total spinal blockade.

4.3 List 3 complications which can arise in the use of this. (3 marks)
